topic: Multifunctional Hybrid Surface Topographies for Full Protection in Guided Bone Regeneration
title: Multifunctional Hybrid Surface Topographies for Full Protection in Guided Bone Regeneration
session_title: Biomaterials: Graduate Student Award Session (Invited Talks)
abstract: Implant-associated complications—including infections, immune responses, and insufficient tissue integration—pose substantial risks to patients, often leading to implant failure or the need for revision surgeries. Traditional chemical-based approaches, such as antibiotic coatings, face challenges due to limited effectiveness, narrow therapeutic windows, and potential toxicity. Surface topography has emerged as a promising alternative, yet most designs are tailored to single cell types and do not fully account for the dynamic, multicellular interactions at the implant–host interface. In this study, we introduce a multifunctional platform featuring hybrid nano-micro wrinkled topographies, fabricated using a bottom-up nanomanufacturing process. This system simultaneously targets bacteria, immune cells, and tissue progenitors, promoting antibacterial action, immune regulation, and tissue regeneration. Through co-culture models and transcriptomic analysis, we demonstrate that nanoscale features hinder bacterial adhesion, while microscale features facilitate macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation via mechanotransduction. Macrophages exhibit context-dependent behavior, switching between pro-inflammatory responses during infection and anti-inflammatory responses for tissue repair, thereby creating a balanced immune environment conducive to implant integration. The flexible and modular nature of this platform offers a versatile solution for developing next-generation biomaterials applicable to diverse medical applications. I also wish my abstract to be considered for the Biomaterials Graduate Student Award Session. topic: 3D Printed of Shilajit (Natural Herb) Reinforced with Polyvinyl Alcohol/Carboxymethyl Cellulose for Biomedical Applications
title: 3D Printed of Shilajit (Natural Herb) Reinforced with Polyvinyl Alcohol/Carboxymethyl Cellulose for Biomedical Applications
abstract: The present study developed a novel 3D-printed scaffold reinforced with shilajit, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) to examine its structural, rheological, and biological properties. The mineral substance, shilajit, was purified using hydrofluoric acid and subsequently blended with the CMC/PVA composite. Optical images confirmed the scaffold's favorable layer fidelity and inter-crosslinked porous structure. The CMC/PVA/Shilajit scaffold exhibited excellent antibacterial efficacy against Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), which may be attributed to its content of fulvic acid, humic acid, and trace minerals. FTIR analysis of the 3D-printed scaffolds revealed distinct profiles with limited sharp bands, confirming the successful binding of shilajit within the matrix. The crosslinked scaffolds demonstrated desirable swelling ability, biodegradability, and antibacterial activity, making them promising candidates for potential skin regeneration applications.

topic: QM/MM Elucidation of the Catalytic Mechanism of PHA Synthase
title: QM/MM Elucidation of the Catalytic Mechanism of PHA Synthase
abstract: The global surge in plastic waste continues to threaten ecosystems due to inefficient recycling and improper waste management. Despite the continuous increase in plastic production, a significant portion of plastic remains unrecycled and ends up being incinerated, landfilled, or improperly managed. This crisis has intensified the need for biodegradable alternatives. Among them, polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) has emerged as a particularly promising candidate due to its biodegradability in both soil and marine environments. Despite its advantages, low productivity remains a major barrier to PHA’s widespread adoption. To enhance PHA production, it is essential to refine both the microbial systems and the catalytic properties of PHA synthase, which drives the polymerization process. In this study, we investigated the catalytic mechanism of Class I PHA synthase using QM/MM metadynamics at the PBE/MM MD level, incorporating a large QM region to capture key interactions. The enzyme utilizes 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA (3HB-CoA) as the monomeric substrate, and its catalytic triad, HIS-CYS-ASP was analyzed in detail. The reaction mechanism involves proton transfer from Cys118 to His307, concerted with a nucleophilic attack by Cys118 on the substrate, leading to the release of CoA. Subsequently, another 3HB-CoA is inserted into the active site, and the elongation of 3HB occurs through the same process. The first nucleophilic attack was identified as the rate-determining step with an activation barrier of ~12 kcal/mol. Additionally, we evaluated two competing elongation pathways—one involving His307 and another involving Asp279. Our findings indicate a clear preference for the Asp279-mediated pathway. To support these insights, DFT calculations on an isolated active site model were performed and compared with the QM/MM results. This work enhances our understanding of the catalytic mechanism of PHA synthase and paves the way for further rational enzyme engineering efforts.

topic: From Self-Assembly to Function: Probing Living Biomaterials Via Advanced X-Ray Scattering
title: From Self-Assembly to Function: Probing Living Biomaterials Via Advanced X-Ray Scattering
abstract: Nature has long optimized spatial organization to enable efficient function; whether as channels for transport, barriers for protection, or interfaces for catalysis. Prokaryotic cells, though unicellular and structurally simple, exhibit elegant examples of such organization through lipid membranes and protein assemblies that sustain life and drive metabolism. In the pursuit of sustainable materials, microbes offer an exciting platform for polymer synthesis. Certain bacteria and archaea can produce polyesters such as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) from carbon dioxide or simple sugars, and these polymers can make up more than half of the cell’s biomass. My research explores how to harness these biologically synthesized polyesters by embedding the living microbes within hydrogel matrices, creating living biomaterials that combine biological activity with engineered structure. Using advanced materials characterization techniques, including synchrotron-based X-ray scattering, confocal laser scanning microscopy, and atomic force microscopy, we investigate how intracellular polymer synthesis affects the mechanical and structural properties of the composite material. Given water’s role as a plasticizer, we also apply interfacial energy strategies to modulate polymer crystallinity which is crucial for tuning mechanical and thermal behavior. This talk will present a materials-science-driven platform to systematically study and design living biomaterials for energy and health applications, bridging microbial metabolism, soft materials, and polymer physics.

topic: Cellulose Nanofiber-Based Gut-like Bioreactor for the Production of Multi-Strain Anaerobic Probiotic Formulations
title: Cellulose Nanofiber-Based Gut-like Bioreactor for the Production of Multi-Strain Anaerobic Probiotic Formulations
abstract: The human gut is home to a complex community of microbes that affect health by influencing digestion, immune function, and neurophysiology. Dysbiosis, an imbalance in this community, is linked to several intestinal disorders (including obesity and inflammatory bowel disease) which are on a trend of increasing prevalence. Probiotics have gained attention for their utility in maintaining gut health and treating intestinal disorders. However, limited cultivation of critical gut microbes has led to most probiotics being limited to single or oligo-strain formulations, with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus spp . dominating the probiotic market due to their historical use in the food industry. Consequently, the therapeutic potential of probiotics is limited by low metabolic and taxonomic diversity of commercial preparations. The development of probiotic treatments is also challenged by the required encapsulation within hydrogel materials to ensure viability and targeted delivery within the gut, which increases production costs and can be counterproductive for multi-strain probiotic formulations. Here, a novel, yet frugal, radial in situ fibrous bed bioreactor ( is FBB)-fermentation approach is introduced that merges probiotic encapsulation with simultaneous multi-species fermentation to produce high-viability multi-strain probiotics for a panel of 10 anaerobic gut commensal species. In this work, the underlying assumptions were tested with optical and electron microscopy and results demonstrate how is FBB technology mimics the gut microenvironment, facilitating the development of novel multi-strain probiotics formulation through a scalable, sustainable, and cost-effective system. This technology shows potential to enhance the production of personalized probiotics, especially for low-and middle-income countries, and in advancing gut microbiome research.

topic: Synergistic Effect of Chlorella sorokiniana and Neem Leaves on Corrosion Inhibition of Steel in Alkaline Medium
title: Synergistic Effect of Chlorella sorokiniana and Neem Leaves on Corrosion Inhibition of Steel in Alkaline Medium
abstract: Corrosion of steel in alkaline environments, particularly in reinforced concrete, remains a critical challenge due to its economic, safety, and environmental repercussions. While conventional corrosion inhibitors offer mitigation, their ecological footprint necessitates sustainable alternatives. This study explores the synergistic potential of Chlorella sorokiniana (microalgae) and neem leaf extract ( Azadirachta indica ) as a green, biodegradable corrosion inhibitor for steel in alkaline media (pH 12.5). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization revealed a remarkable inhibition efficiency of 92% when combining 200 ppm neem extract with C. sorokiniana biofilm, outperforming individual components (75% for neem alone, 68% for microalgae alone). Weight loss measurements corroborated these findings, showing a corrosion rate reduction from 0.148 mm/year (unprotected steel) to 0.012 mm/year with the dual inhibitor system. Surface characterization via SEM confirmed the formation of a dense, adherent protective layer, while XPS analysis identified synergistic interactions between neem-derived phytochemicals (e.g., azadirachtin, nimbin) and algal extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), which facilitated passivation through chelation with Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ions. The hybrid inhibitor also demonstrated stability over 30 days, with minimal efficiency loss (<5%), highlighting its durability. This work establishes a paradigm for eco-friendly corrosion mitigation, combining renewable biological resources to enhance material longevity in infrastructure applications while aligning with global sustainability goals.

topic: Machine Learning–Driven Optimization of Ionizable Lipids for High-Efficiency mRNA Delivery to Liver and Gene Editing in the Lung Epithelia
title: Machine Learning–Driven Optimization of Ionizable Lipids for High-Efficiency mRNA Delivery to Liver and Gene Editing in the Lung Epithelia
abstract: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, delivered via lipid nanoparticles or LNPs has emerged as a transformative platform for a wide range of therapeutic applications, from protein replacement to correcting genetic disorders. The clinical success of the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines truly brought this technology into the spotlight. Building on that foundation, our research aims to develop next-generation mRNA delivery systems to treat chronic diseases—particularly those affecting the liver and lungs, such as Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and cystic fibrosis. We started by targeting liver delivery. To do this, we synthesized a library of 384 novel ester-derived biodegradable ionizable lipids. To minimize animal use, especially C57BL/6 mice, we developed a high-throughput in vivo screening platform using peptide-barcoded mRNA. This allowed us to test LNP formulations systematically. From 24 different formulations, we identified one that achieved a threefold increase in liver transfection efficiency compared to our original benchmark. We then validated these findings using a human erythropoietin (hEPO) expression assay. Impressively, our lead biodegradable lipid delivered mRNA to the liver 4.5 times more effectively than DLin-MC3-DMA—a clinically validated standard. To push the efficiency even further, we introduced a deep learning–based platform we call LiON—short for Lipid Optimization using Neural Networks. Trained on a dataset of over 9,000 mRNA delivery outcomes from both in vitro and in vivo studies, LiON could accurately predict top-performing lipids. It identified lipids like RJ-A30-T01, which not only outperformed existing clinical lipids like MC3 and SM-102, but also validated the strength of AI-guided design in this space. Shifting focus to lung delivery, we sought to enable CRISPR-Cas9–based gene editing in the lungs. We designed a three-component delivery system and synthesized more than 700 biodegradable lipids. Using Cre-recombinase mRNA in Ai9 tdTomato reporter mice, we achieved up to 53% tdTomato-positive cells—double what we previously saw with nebulized Cre-mRNA. Finally, RCB-4-8 LNPs, when loaded with Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA at low and high doses and quantified gene-editing, could result in 3 and 7% tdTomato+ cells, respectively. These Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA loaded mRNA were found to gene editing in both club cells and ciliated cells. Application of these CRISPR-Cas9 mRNA for gene/cancer therapy by removing faulty genes or correcting mutations is ongoing.

topic: Engineering Biomimetic Materials: Nanotechnology Inspired By Biology
title: Engineering Biomimetic Materials: Nanotechnology Inspired By Biology
abstract: Nature inspires the design of synthetic polymers that replicate optical, biological, and structural features, enabling their application across energy, life sciences, and medicine. I believe in the power of polymer chemistry to mimic the functional properties of biomolecules, enabling precise control of interactions at nano-bio interfaces and responsiveness to target biomolecules. In this talk, I will introduce enzyme-responsive biomolecular condensates and their potential in smart drug delivery. 1 I have developed size-tunable coacervates through the self-assembly of heparin glycosaminoglycans with tyrosine- and arginine-based peptides. By incorporating thrombin recognition sites into the structural components, these coacervates can be selectively disassembled upon thrombin-mediated proteolysis. Furthermore, I discovered a critical polyphenol threshold that enhances the stability of biomolecular condensates while preserving their enzymatic activity. Lastly, I will present emerging techniques for the development of biomimetic materials and discuss their applications in the field of biomedical engineering. 2,3,4,5 Reference: 1. topic: Nucleic Acid Cytometry of Rare Intact HIV Reservoir Cells
title: Nucleic Acid Cytometry of Rare Intact HIV Reservoir Cells
abstract: In the U.S., approximately 1.2 million individuals are living with HIV, with 38,100 new diagnoses reported in 2022 [1]. Managing HIV requires lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART), creating a substantial economic burden that averages $420,000 per patient and totals approximately $2.25 billion annually nationwide [2]. Lifelong ART is required to prevent HIV rebound, which occurs within weeks of treatment interruption from blood and tissue CD4+ T cell reservoirs. Although HIV-infected cells constitute less than 1% of the total CD4+ T cell population, only approximately 0.01% (about 100 per million CD4⁺ T cells) harbor intact, replication-competent proviruses capable of producing infectious virion [3]. This reservoir is considered the primary barrier to a cure, but the molecular mechanisms that control virus persistence remain incompletely understood, primarily due to the difficulty in isolating and studying these exceedingly rare reservoir cells ex vivo. We developed FIND-seq (Focused Interrogation of Cells by Nucleic Acid Detection and Sequencing), a droplet-based microfluidics platform designed to selectively isolate and RNA-sequence rare HIV-infected cells using nucleic acid biomarkers [4]. In this approach, single cells are encapsulated into 50-micron agarose hydrogel beads, and cellular mRNA is reverse-transcribed to cDNA using agarose functionalized oligo dT primers. The cDNA-containing beads are reinjected into droplets containing TaqMan reagents and subjected to thermocycling. Finally, fluorescent droplets are sorted and RNA-sequenced [5]. In its original implementation, FIND-seq targeted a single region of the HIV genome (gag), which was insufficient to differentiate intact from defective proviruses, limiting the application of this technology for reservoir studies. To address this, we implemented the intact proviral DNA assay (IPDA) [3], which uses multiplexed detection of two distinct HIV genomic regions (psi, env). We validated the FIND-seq IPDA assay using a J.Lat 6.3 cell line model of HIV latency that harbors a near-intact provirus, achieving over 90% psi+ env+ detection. To assess the sensitivity of FIND-seq, we successfully recovered the transcriptomes of HIV+ J.Lat cells diluted into HIV- Jurkat cells at frequencies as low as 0.1%. These results demonstrate that FIND-seq can accurately identify and isolate rare HIV-infected cells with intact proviruses, providing a powerful platform for understanding the biology of HIV persistence. topic: Harnessing Evolution for Protein Design to Address Public Health Challenges
title: Harnessing Evolution for Protein Design to Address Public Health Challenges
abstract: During natural evolution, viral proteins can mutate to gain new properties that help them survive within and spread to different hosts. Owing to the massive surveillance data on viral sequences that cause infectious diseases, we can learn from natural selection by mapping viral genomic sequences to protein functions using machine learning. Using influenza virus as an example, I demonstrated a novel machine learning classifier capable of predicting key viral protein functions, trained solely on naturally occurring (positive-only) influenza sequences. The accuracy of this model was first verified using site-directed mutagenesis data from the literature and it achieved superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches from the one-class classification (OCC) and positive-unlabeled (PU) learning literature. I further demonstrated experimentally that de novo protein sequences predicted by the our model exhibited influenza viral functions of interests. By integrating machine learning with domain-specific biochemistry knowledge of protein evolution, our work shows great promise in predicting viral variants of concern for disease surveillance and in assisting protein design for disease prevention and therapeutics.

topic: Biophysical Engineering of Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes Via Contact-Dependent Phosphatase Exclusion Using Micropatches
title: Biophysical Engineering of Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes Via Contact-Dependent Phosphatase Exclusion Using Micropatches
abstract: Despite decades of innovation in cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL)–based therapies, their efficacy in solid tumors remains limited compared to the remarkable success of CAR T cells in hematologic malignancies. A key barrier is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which restricts CTL accessibility and rapidly diminishes their effector function, often within hours of infusion, even in cells primed ex vivo with robust cytotoxic and proliferative capacity. Therefore, strategies that sustain CTL functionality post-transfer are of interest to increase their therapeutic potential in solid tumors. Here, we present a novel cell-surface engineering approach leveraging contact-driven CD45-phosphatase exclusion, a biomaterial-based strategy that modulates CTL phenotype and sustains their functionality post-infusion. We engineered micron-scale polymeric micropatches fabricated from either polylactic-co-glycolide (PLGA) or hyaluronic acid (HA), both biopolymers with demonstrated clinical compatibility. These micropatches bind efficiently to CTLs, and, upon contact, induce spatial exclusion of CD45 phosphatase at the CTL contact interface. This exclusion was validated through diffusion-signaling-based mathematical modeling and high-resolution imaging, establishing it as a biochemical mechanism for tonic CTL stimulation, an effect that conventional nanoparticle configurations failed to achieve. Notably, this stimulation was observed to occur independent of the specific material used or receptor engaged, suggesting a platform-agnostic mechanism driven solely by contact-mediated reorganization at the CTL surface. We focused on PLGA-based micropatches, termed PMPEs (Polymeric Micropatches for Phosphatase Exclusion), and demonstrated through bulk RNA sequencing that PMPE modification induces transcriptomic changes consistent with enhanced CTL effector potential. A comprehensive array of in vitro assays, including ELISA, calcium flux, immunofluorescence, proliferation, and cytotoxicity, alongside in vivo studies (biodistribution, immunophenotyping, pathology), revealed that PMPE-CTLs exhibit enhanced persistence, robust Type 1 immunostimulatory response, and excellent tolerability. In aggressive B16F10 melanoma models, PMPE-CTLs significantly improved tumor control, with 50% survival beyond 25 days, compared to no survival in unmodified CTLs. When combined with systemic IL-15 superagonist (IL15sa) therapy, PMPE-CTLs extended survival beyond 35 days in 46% of mice, with 15.4% achieving complete remission, a result not observed in the IL15sa + CTL group alone. Altogether, this work introduces a contact-driven cell engineering strategy as a simple, scalable, and drug-free biomaterial-based approach to modulate CTL behavior and sustain their functionality within hostile tumor microenvironments. Remarkably, this effect is achieved even with blank microparticles, without the need for conventional drug loading. The platform is readily compatible with existing clinical manufacturing workflows, offering a simple yet effective avenue for advancing the development of next-generation CTL therapies for solid tumor management.

topic: Analysis of the Polystyrene Conversion to the High-Quality Battery-Grade Graphite By Two Stage Thermal Treatment Process
title: Analysis of the Polystyrene Conversion to the High-Quality Battery-Grade Graphite By Two Stage Thermal Treatment Process
abstract: Sustainable energy storage solutions, such as Li-ion batteries (LIBs) , play an important role in the green transition, a shift towards economically sustainable growth and an economy that is not based on fossil fuels and overconsumption of natural resources. However, current battery markets are strongly dependent on the availability of critical raw materials (CRM). While demand for CRM is projected to increase drastically, Europe and USA heavily rely on imports, often from quasi-monopolistic third-country suppliers nowadays. China currently controls more than 75% of the world overall battery manufactory capability. Especially the situation with overall production of battery-grade graphite looks critical as most of it (about 87%) is produced in China. Moreover, globally the natural resources of graphite are limited, and graphite reserves are estimated to be ∼ 300 million tons, with Turkey holding the largest share at ∼ 30%, followed by Brazil and China at ∼ 24% each. Mozambique, Tanzania, and India also contribute, with shares of ∼ 5.7, 5.7 and ∼ 2.7%, respectively [1]. Because of this, in its latest European Commission proposals the graphite was named as a critical raw material and battery-grade graphite as a strategic raw material [2]. It is obvious that increasing battery-grade graphite production in Europe and in the USA is critically important to mitigate risks of disruptions to the supply of battery-grade graphite and improve circularity and sustainability. However, the concentration of attention on production of the battery-grade graphite from natural graphite or non-renewable carbonaceous precursor such as petroleum coke, pitch coke and natural gas cannot be considered as the solution of the problem because of the non-availability the significant amount of required non-renewable carbonaceous precursor in Europe and USA, which significantly increases the cost and decreases the sustainability of this process. Therefore, consideration of other possible carbonaceous precursors for the battery grade graphite production in Europe and USA is necessary. Plastic waste can be a suitable precursor for battery-grade graphite production. Currently, 4.9 billion tons of plastic waste have been accumulated in the natural environment and this number was estimated to reach around 13 billion tons worldwide by 2050 since ~300 million tons of plastic are generated annually. The worldwide plastic production is calculated to be 400.3 million tons in 2022 [3]. Despite the recycling has been growing steadily over the last 30 years, about 15 % of plastic waste is recycled from annual waste production [4]. Moreover, it usually requires a considerable amount of money to do a disposal and recycling of plastic that may not be financially feasible for underdeveloped countries [3]. Also, currently existing waste plastic utilization methods, for example incineration, can release harmful byproducts into the environment. Because of this, the development of low-cost and environmentally friendly utilization methods for plastic waste to high-added cost chemical feedstock and novel materials that can be utilized preferably in high-tech added value applications will be highly desirable. Such method should be more environmentally friendly than incineration and more economically attractive than currently existing plastic recycling methods, which focused on obtaining gas-liquid products and using it on synthesis of various motor fuels, because of the small yield of solid residue in the plastic pyrolysis [5] . The conversion of the waste plastic in battery grade graphite is a promising solution as it satisfies all requirements. In current work we investigated the applicability of waste plastic such as polystyrene (PS) as precursor for the production of the battery grade graphite. The PS was pre-carbonized before graphitization at high inert (N 2 )-pressure reactor. To achieve the high yield from the PS carbonization, the treatment conditions such as temperature, pressure and holding time were optimized. Moreover, a small amount of reduced graphene oxide was mixed with PS. The optimization of the PS pre-carbonization process increases the carbon yield up to about 60 wt.% of the initial mass of PS. The further graphitization of the material was done at 2400 o C during 2h. The iron oxide was used as a catalyst to perform catalytic graphitization process. The morphology and particle size of iron oxide were optimized. The effect of the catalyst particle size in the diapason from 10 nm to 1000 nm of the catalytic graphitization process was thoroughly analyzed. The structural, compositional, and morphological properties of the materials created after high pressure carbonization and catalytic graphitization are investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Sigma HDVP) and the energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The amount of the catalysts and additivities in the obtained materials before catalytic graphitization will be characterized by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) (Q50 TA instruments). The structural defects in the material after catalytic graphitization will be analysed by using Raman spectrometry (Thermo DXR2xi with a λ=532 nm laser). The X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) data will be collected on a Bruker AXS D8 Advance equipped with monochromatized Cu Kα. The interlayer spacing ( d 002 ) was determined using the Bragg's equation, the graphitization degree was determined using the Franklin equation, and the crystallite size ( L a ) and the stacking height ( L c ) were evaluated using the Scherrer formula. Electrochemical testing of graphite structures will be done by using coin-cells with metallic lithium counter electrodes. The water-soluble binder e.g., styrene-butadiene rubber/carboxymethyl cellulose binder, will be used for the graphite electrode creation. The 1 M LiPF6 in 1:1 EC:DMC electrolyte and glass microfiber fiber separator (Whatman GF/A) will be used for the coin cell creation. The electrochemical characterization of the created coin cells will be done after formation and will include cyclic voltammetry (CV) and galvanostatic charge-discharge curves at different C-rate currents. The results currently obtained showed the possibility to produce high-quality graphite from PS by applying two step treatment processes including high pressure carbonization and catalytic graphitization processes. The obtained material has a high degree of graphitization and crystallite size ( L a ) and the stacking height ( L c ), obtained after XRD spectra analysis, correspond to the commercial graphite. The Raman analysis showed relatively low I D /I G peak ratio and good D and G peaks separation, which indicates low level of structural disorder and defects and high ordered structure. TGA analysis showed the good purity of the obtained material, which is equal to 99.5% as can be seen in Figure 1 (c). The produced materials have close to commercial graphite electrochemical properties. The reversible specific capacity of the PS-based graphite was equal to 344.5 mAh/g at 0.1 C and initial columbic efficiency (ICE) without addition of vinylene carbonate (VC) to electrolyte was 81.92% (Fig 1. topic: a Deep Learning Framework for Antibody-Antigen Interface Prediction
title: a Deep Learning Framework for Antibody-Antigen Interface Prediction
abstract: Accurately identifying antibody-antigen binding interfaces is essential for therapeutic antibody development and immunological research, yet remains a significant challenge due to structural heterogeneity, sparse interface residues, and severe class imbalance. Previous approaches have attempted to address these issues through heuristic downsampling, complementarity-determining region (CDR)-only input, or transfer learning. However, these strategies often suffer from limited generalization or discarded contextual information. We introduce MGI (Masked Graph Interface Predictor), a deep learning framework that integrates sequence embeddings, graph neural networks (GNNs), and self-attention to model antibody-antigen interactions with improved contextual awareness. MGI features two key innovations: Dynamic Masking (DyM), which adaptively focuses on informative residues while suppressing irrelevant signals; and Gradient Shift Descent (GSD), a novel optimization method that incorporates auxiliary structural features to escape poor local minima and enhances existing transfer learning pipelines. MGI achieves state-of-the-art epitope prediction performance, with the AUC-PR surpassing the previous best performance by about 20%. Moreover, we demonstrate that paratope prediction can be accurately performed using antibody-only input. These findings underscore MGI’s potential to advance computational immunology and accelerate structure-based vaccine design.

topic: Comparative Economic Analysis of Methanol Production Pathways: Evaluating Feedstock Viability for Cost-Effective Synthesis
title: Comparative Economic Analysis of Methanol Production Pathways: Evaluating Feedstock Viability for Cost-Effective Synthesis
abstract: Methanol serves as a crucial chemical energy carrier, exhibiting extensive applications in fuel production and functioning as a precursor to essential industrial chemicals, including acetic acid and formaldehyde. Considering its increasing significance in sustainable energy and chemical manufacturing, the optimization of methanol production pathways is essential. The current study undertakes a comprehensive economic evaluation of methanol production utilizing three different feedstocks: (1) carbon dioxide and hydrogen (CO₂/H₂), (2) natural gas, and (3) biomass. A comprehensive evaluation framework was utilized to analyze capital expenditures, energy requirements, methanol yield value, and payback periods, integrating heat recovery to improve process efficiency. The findings demonstrate that the production of methanol from natural gas presents the most favourable economic viability, attributed to reduced capital and operational expenditures. Conversely, the CO₂/H₂ pathway entails considerably elevated expenses attributed to the energy-demanding processes of hydrogen production and carbon capture. Nonetheless, this pathway presents significant environmental benefits by employing CO₂ as a feedstock, thereby aiding decarbonization initiatives within the chemical sector. The economic implications of biomass-derived methanol are characterized by intermediate challenges, as costs are affected by the variability of feedstock and the intricacies of processing methods. This study offers practical insights for stakeholders aiming to reconcile economic viability with sustainability goals in methanol production. The results emphasize that natural gas represents the most economically viable feedstock given the present market circumstances, while also indicating the necessity for technological innovations and policy backing to enhance the competitiveness of CO₂-based pathways.

topic: Machine Learning of Molecular Biophysics to Transformatively Augment Low-N Protein Engineering
title: Machine Learning of Molecular Biophysics to Transformatively Augment Low-N Protein Engineering
abstract: Protein engineering has been greatly accelerated by the application of machine learning (ML) to building mutation effect prediction models: tools trained to accurately predict the downstream effects of one or more mutations on protein functions of interest. Despite the promise of this emerging field, a principal limitation of ML for predicting mutation effects is the availability of large datasets of experimentally determined mutation effects for use as training data. Furthermore, even the strongest mutation effect prediction models are unable to offer interpretable mechanistic explanations for predicted changes in protein functions. Here, I develop an approach to protein mutation effect prediction that greatly reduces the amount of experimental data required to obtain accurate predictions, while also providing molecular-level explanations of those effects. This approach is based on combining traditional mutation effect prediction models with dynamic, biophysical information obtained from molecular dynamics simulations of hundreds or thousands of protein variants. I first explain the rationale and design of the method, and then demonstrate that this approach greatly reduces the amount of experimental data needed to arrive at high-quality functional predictions across two highly distinct proteins and functions . Then, I show how model predictions of protein dynamics provide a framework for interpreting the predictions of the model in the context of physically meaningful molecular quantities. Excitingly, the model is able to identify key residues mediating protein-protein binding interactions based on simulations of just one protein, by correlating molecular-level effects with benchtop binding affinity data. This work establishes a new, highly practical alternative to the collection of large experimental datasets for training protein mutation effect models, opens a new avenue for systematically rationalizing and quantifying the molecular underpinnings of arbitrary protein functions, and lays the foundation for a data-efficient combined computational and experimental approach to ML-guided protein engineering.

topic: High Yield, Green Synthesis of ZIF Nanoparticles for Efficient Treatment of Pharmaceutical Wastewater: Parametric Study
title: High Yield, Green Synthesis of ZIF Nanoparticles for Efficient Treatment of Pharmaceutical Wastewater: Parametric Study
abstract: Zeolitic imidazole frameworks (ZIFs) have gained a lot of attention for wastewater treatment due to their high crystallinity, high surface area, tunable aperture size, and the capability of functionalization. Here in this work, we showcased the impact of addition rates of metal salt precursor to the organic linker solution and different reaction times on the size and morphology of the synthesized ZIF nanoparticles using water as a green solvent. Additionally, the removal efficiency of tetracycline from pharmaceutical wastewater was evaluated to assess its adsorption potential. The scanning electron microscopy revealed the nanoparticles' size and morphology differences due to different reaction times and varying flow rates of the salt precursor. The nanoparticles demonstrated a high yield of approximately 92%. Further, adsorption studies were carried out, and the particles prepared with optimized parameters showed a high tetracycline removal efficiency of ~80%. The high adsorption capacity of the nanoparticles can be attributed to their microporous nature and surface functionality. Interestingly, the prepared ZIF nanoadsorbents showed excellent reusability without any regeneration step. In conclusion, this study demonstrates an environmentally friendly method to prepare ZIF nanoparticles at ambient conditions, which hold promise as effective adsorbents for pharmaceutical wastewater treatment.

topic: Use of Discrete Element and Finite Element Methods to Identify Potential Causes of Tablet Defects during Manufacturing
title: Use of Discrete Element and Finite Element Methods to Identify Potential Causes of Tablet Defects during Manufacturing
abstract: Tablet compression is a key step in the commercial production where the powder material is compressed to form the tablet dosage forms. The core tablets are then film coated. Following film coating, the coated tablets are packaged and finally released into the market. The structural integrity of the tablets is an important critical quality attribute. Hence, it is crucial that the tablets are free of any structural defects. There are different types of tablet defects, the common ones being- capping/lamination [1], chipping/erosion [2] and picking/sticking [3]. During manufacturing of the tablets, there are several potential steps that can cause structural defects, e.g., during the compression operation, the film coating operation and the transfer of the tablets from one unit operation to another. Modeling techniques- discrete element model (DEM) and finite element model (FEM) are widely used to model the tablet attributes during film coating [4] and compression [5] operations. Important variables that affect the potential for tablet defects could be the operating parameters, equipment geometry parameters, material properties and tablet design (shape/size). Tablet defects during film coating as a function of the operating parameters, equipment geometry parameters and tablet design have been extensively studied in literature using DEM [4, 6]. Similarly, tablet defects as a function of the compression operating parameters [7] and tablet shape [8] have been studied using FEM. However, there is a gap in investigating aspects of geometrical tolerances in a compression machine (tablet press). A tablet press consists of a punch-die assembly that must be carefully assembled and installed maintaining the correct alignment. The slightest misalignment outside the allowed design tolerance could result in critical tablet defects like capping. In this work, a FEM analysis was used to study the propensity of defect initiation because of punch-die installation errors that might appear small and remain undetected during routine checks. A defect initiated during compression can be exaggerated during the downstream unit operations. Therefore, a DEM was used to model the tablet flow during transfer of the tablet cores stored in an intermediate bulk container (after the compression) into the coating pan. The model results were used to make inferences on the propensity of tablet defect exaggeration during the transfer. This work highlights the importance of inspection and following the right protocol for assembling equipment during tablet manufacturing operation. References: 1. J. Meynard, F. Amado-Becker, P. topic: Assessing Molecular Doping Efficiency in Organic Semiconductors
title: Assessing Molecular Doping Efficiency in Organic Semiconductors
abstract: The addition of molecular dopants into organic semiconductors (OSCs) is a ubiquitous augmentation strategy to enhance the electrical conductivity of OSCs. Chemically generalizable structure–function relationships are difficult to extract due to the sensitive dependence of doping efficiency on both charge transfer and charge transport processes. Computational modeling provides a powerful paradigm to isolate fundamental relationships for integrated OSC–dopant design, but requires the simultaneous treatment of electronic structure, molecular reactivity, morphology evolution. We present the first computational study to couple molecular reactivity with morphology evolution in a molecularly doped OSC. Using reactive Monte Carlo, we observe that for well-mixed systems with experimentally relevant dielectric constants, doping efficiency is near unity with a very weak dependence on the ionization potential and electron affinity of OSC and dopant, respectively. To clarify the role of the electronic driving force and justify the observed doping efficiencies, we utilize density functional theory calculations to correlate the energetic difference in frontier molecular orbitals of the OSC and dopant species to the extent of charge transferred between them. We establish the importance of the strength of the Coulombic interaction between the two species in lowering the energetic barrier for ground-state charge transfer. Furthermore, our simulations reproduce the well-known insolubility of solution-doped materials: reaction-induced aggregation reduces the doping efficiency, highlighting a key design criterion for maximizing doping efficiency. In summary, this work pioneers the systematic integration of electronic structure, molecular reactivity, and morphology evolution into the characterization of multi-scale structure–function relationships in molecularly doped OSCs.

topic: Design of Ion-Sieve for Selective Adsorption of Lithium from Geothermal Brine
title: Design of Ion-Sieve for Selective Adsorption of Lithium from Geothermal Brine
abstract: The growing demand for lithium-ion batteries necessitates efficient and sustainable lithium extraction technologies. Geothermal brines provide an alternative lithium source; however, their complex ionic composition challenges selective lithium recovery. Hydrogen manganese oxides (H 4 Mn 4.5 O 12 ) are widely studied as lithium-ion sieves due to their high selectivity for lithium ions. Still, its structural instability and manganese dissolution during adsorption-desorption cycles limit long-term performance. This study introduced zirconium (Zr) doping into the spinel-type Li 4 Mn 5 O 12 precursor through a one-step calcination process (450 °C for 24 hours at 10 °C min −1 ), ensuring an energy-efficient synthesis process of Li 4 Mn 4.5 Zr 0.5 O 12 (LMZO) matrix. The resulting spinel H 4 Mn 4.5 Zr 0.5 O 12 (HMZO), after acid activation, underwent comprehensive characterization employing several analytical techniques, including Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The HMZO exhibited a lithium adsorption capacity of 26.81 mg/g in synthetic brine, with a maximum capacity of 35 mg/g at an adsorbent-to-solution ratio of 0.017 g/50 mL, while restricting manganese dissolution to 0.78% after five adsorption-desorption cycles. Adsorption kinetics followed the pseudo-second-order model, while the Freundlich isotherm indicated a heterogeneous Li-H ion exchange mechanism. The thermodynamic analysis confirmed that lithium adsorption was endothermic and entropy-driven, improving with increased temperature. These findings highlight the enhanced stability and reusability of HMZO, demonstrating its potential as a next-generation lithium-ion sieve for sustainable lithium recovery from geothermal brines. Further optimization, including refining zirconium content and activation conditions, is necessary to maximize long-term adsorption performance.

topic: Purification By Temperature Swing Adsorption Technology
title: Purification By Temperature Swing Adsorption Technology
abstract: Chemical Design specializes in designing advanced adsorption systems, providing sustainable and efficient solutions for purifying and recovering specific components from gas or liquid mixtures. One of the key advantages of adsorption over other separation methods is its ability to selectively capture specific molecules, even at trace concentrations. As global attention shifts towards sustainability and resource recovery, Chemical Design’s adsorption systems are gaining recognition for their energy efficiency and regenerative capability. These advantages make adsorption a preferred solution in many industrial applications worldwide. Industry Applications Chemical Design’s adsorption systems are employed across a wide range of industries, with several critical applications in everyday operations: Hydrogen Purification: Production of high-purity hydrogen, which is used in clean energy technologies, such as fuel cells for transportation, stationary power generation, and as a clean alternative to fossil fuels in industrial operations. Additionally, hydrogen purification is essential for its use in the electronics, refining, and chemical production industries. Air Separation: Production of purified nitrogen and oxygen, which are indispensable in various manufacturing industries for providing controlled atmospheres. Oxygen is also vital in the healthcare industry for readily available supply. Natural Gas Treatment: Removal of impurities such as water, sulfur, carbon dioxide, and heavy hydrocarbons ensuring that the gas meets the necessary quality standards for either safe transport or consumption. Purified natural gas is then used for residential heating, electricity generation, and various industrial applications. Chemicals and Petrochemicals: Purification of solvents to ensure high-quality for use in chemical processes, as well as the removal of contaminants from petrochemical feedstocks to produce high-purity end products in various industrial applications. How Adsorption Works Adsorption occurs when a gas or liquid comes into contact with the surface of a solid adsorbent. Typically, the adsorbent is a porous material with a high surface area that attracts target molecules in the fluid phase. This attraction occurs through physical interactions, such as van der Waals forces. These forces are strong enough for adsorption, yet weak enough to allow for the removal of adsorbed molecules. In standard operations, the adsorbent is packed into a fixed bed. The fluid passes through the bed, leaving contaminants bound to the adsorbent’s surface. Over time, the adsorbent reaches equilibrium, meaning all adsorption sites are occupied and no more contaminants can bind. The difference in concentration (for liquids) or partial pressure (for gases) through the bed drives mass transfer to occur, allowing contaminants to find the next available adsorption site. The equilibrium portion of the bed grows, and the mass transfer zone, where adsorption occurs, advances through the bed. Once most of the bed reaches equilibrium, the bed has reached saturation, and the contaminants must be removed. Regeneration Adsorption is a reversible process, enabling the adsorbent to be regenerated and reused. Chemical Design specializes in a regeneration technique known as Temperature Swing Adsorption (TSA), where heat is applied to the saturated adsorbent to reduce its adsorptive capacity and facilitate the desorption of the target molecules. The desorption process can be described using an equilibrium model, called an isotherm. These models illustrate the amount of adsorbate adsorbed as a function of partial pressure or concentration at a fixed temperature. As the temperature is elevated, equilibrium shifts, causing the adsorbate to be released from the adsorbent. Due to its regenerative nature, TSA operates in a dynamic, cyclic manner. In a typical cycle, adsorption takes place for a set duration until the adsorbent becomes fully saturated with contaminants. A small heat stream of product or inert gas is applied to the adsorbent bed to release and remove the captured molecules, which can either be vented or recycled back into the process for a zero-loss system. Once regeneration is complete, the bed is cooled, and the cycle begins again. Adsorbent Selection Materials such as activated alumina, activated carbon, zeolites, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are commonly used in adsorption due to their high surface area and specific affinity for different molecules. Ongoing research aims to enhance efficiency, selectivity, stability, and regenerative capacity of adsorbents. Chemical Design carefully considers several crucial factors in the selection process that significantly influence the adsorbent’s performance, including: Isotherm Shape: The adsorption isotherm shape indicates how the adsorbent interacts with gases at different pressures and temperatures. Adsorbents with steep isotherms in the operating range can adsorb more molecules at higher pressures, improving their effectiveness in gas separations. Working Capacity: The working capacity refers to the amount of target molecules an adsorbent can hold during the adsorption process, which is influenced by the temperature difference between the feed and regeneration streams. A higher working capacity allows for more efficient use of the adsorbent and better process throughput. Selectivity: Selectivity measures the adsorbent’s ability to preferentially capture one molecule over another. High selectivity ensures that the adsorbent preferentially captures the target molecules, which is highly important in applications requiring high purity. Heat of Adsorption: The heat of adsorption defines how strongly the adsorbate is bound to the adsorbent surface. Adsorbents with lower heats of adsorption are typically more energy-efficient, requiring less energy to regenerate. Lower regeneration temperatures reduce energy consumption and operation costs. Sorption Kinetics: Sorption kinetics describe how quickly can adsorb and desorb target molecules. Faster kinetics provides better dynamic performance, which is essential for maximizing throughput and efficiency in TSA systems. TSA Advantages TSA technology offers several key advantages, with energy efficiency being a standout benefit. By leveraging the exothermic nature of the adsorption process, TSA reduces the overall energy input required for regeneration. Increasing the regeneration gas temperature allows for a smaller regeneration gas rate when compared to other technologies. Additionally, TSA can utilize waste heat to achieve significant energy and cost savings. Beyond energy efficiency, TSA systems are highly effective in achieving ultra-high purity, with the capability to reach low parts per million (ppm) solute levels. This advantage makes TSA ideal for industries that demand stringent purity standards. Alternative separation technologies, such as distillation, can be much more energy intensive. Distillation requires constant heating and cooling of large volumes of liquid to separate components based on their boiling points, which leads to significant amounts of energy consumption and higher operation costs. Additionally, distillation faces inherent limitations in product purity due to the formation of azeotropes, which occur when two or more components form a constant boiling point, preventing further separation. This limitation makes it unsuitable for applications requiring high purity. Closing Thoughts As industries continue to seek solutions to reduce their environmental impact and improve energy efficiency, Chemical Design’s expertise in designing Temperature Swing Adsorption systems presents an effective solution that meets these requirements. The ability to selectively capture specific molecules, coupled with energy-efficient regeneration processes, positions Chemical Design at the forefront of sustainable industrial operations. Continued advancements in adsorbent materials and regeneration techniques will further enhance the performance of adsorption systems, ensuring they remain at the forefront of separation technologies.

abstract: Quantum chemical mechanistic studies may influence the discovery of chemically stable drug candidates and the optimization of synthetic processes. Our study also underscores the accuracy required to guide experiments effectively, discusses the necessity of microsolvation and accuracy of COSMO-RS theory towards solubility estimation.

topic: Mechanistic Modeling of the Formation of Incomplete and Mispaired Multispecific Antibodies
title: Mechanistic Modeling of the Formation of Incomplete and Mispaired Multispecific Antibodies
abstract: Multispecific antibodies are a novel class of therapeutic drug molecules that can simultaneously bind multiple targets. Unlike that of traditional monospecific antibodies, the immunoglobulin chains forming the structure of a multispecific antibody are heterogeneous. As such, correct intracellular assembly is critical to the formation of the desired target molecule. Despite protein engineering efforts to favor the correct configuration, incomplete fragments and mispaired species are still commonly observed in the manufacturing of multispecifics, leading to higher levels of low molecular weight (LMW) impurities that are difficult to clear. To address this challenge, we present a practical mechanistic model that captures the process of mispaired species and LMW formation. After calibration with experimental data, the model can be used for in silico optimizations, nominating conditions that minimize the unwanted impurities. Overall, our work illustrates an example of how mechanistic modeling can accelerate upstream development in new drug modality settings.

topic: Integrated Process Design of Passage Culture and Freezing for Mesenchymal Stem Cells Toward Establishment of Working Cell Banks
title: Integrated Process Design of Passage Culture and Freezing for Mesenchymal Stem Cells Toward Establishment of Working Cell Banks
abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are one of the most promising sources in the field of regenerative medicine such as due to their multipotency and immunosuppression. The cells are widely used in preclinical and clinical regenerative medicine including the treatment of acute graft versus host diseases, type I diabetes mellitus, and chronic liver disease. In MSC manufacturing, cell bank systems are generally accepted as the most practical approach, which consists of two types of cell banks: master cell banks and working cell banks. Master cell banks are developed for the preservation of specific cell lines, while working cell banks store cells that can be used for product manufacturing. For establishment of working cell banks for MSCs, the passage culture and freezing processes are at the core of the cell bank, although there are no clear standards for the design of working cell banks. Hence, working cell banks for MSCs have been designed empirically 1 . In the field of process systems engineering, several regenerative medicine-related processes have been explored by model-based approaches, e.g., cultivation of MSCs 2 and batch freezing of induced pluripotent stem cells 3 . However, these models were limited to unit operations, and it has been difficult to design working cell banks for MSCs with the previously developed models. In this work, an integrated process model of passage culture and freezing for MSCs was newly developed to design the entire passage culture and freezing processes toward establishment of working cell banks for the cells. From a process modeling perspective, it is necessary to consider the impact of the passage culture process on the freezing process. Therefore, we adopted the cell diameter as the connecting variable between the two processes. The cell diameter was expressed as a function of the cumulative population doubling level in the passage culture process model, and the freezing process model calculated the cell survival rate and the number of living cells after thawing using the cell diameter as the input. Given the number of passage operations, the days per passage, and the cooling rate of the freezer, the integrated process model can evaluate the cumulative population doubling level, the cell survival rate, and the number of living cells after thawing. The application of the developed model was demonstrated in a case study. As a result, a feasible parameter range of working cell banks for MSCs was obtained, given a set of constraints which consisted of the cumulative population doubling level, the cell survival rate, and the number of living cells after thawing. These results would be useful for designing working cell banks for MSCs. In the ongoing work, we are conducting probabilistic simulations to obtain a feasible parameter range of working cell banks for MSCs considering uncertainty. References 1. topic: Towards a Multiscale Mechanistic Model of Lipid Nanoparticle Formation
title: Towards a Multiscale Mechanistic Model of Lipid Nanoparticle Formation
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a versatile drug delivery platform for a wide range of therapeutic modalities including nucleic acids which have received much attention for their use in the COVID-19 vaccines. Modern manufacturing processes for LNPs for nucleic acids involve rapidly mixing an organic stream containing the lipids with an aqueous stream containing the nucleic acids and are conceptually straightforward. However, detailed understanding of LNP formation and structure is still limited and scale-up can be challenging. Mathematical and computational methods are a promising avenue for deepening scientific understanding of the LNP formation process and facilitating improved process development and control. In this presentation, a framework for constructing mechanistic models of reactor-scale and particle-scale processes is first outlined. Initial efforts towards developing a detailed mechanistic model are discussed. In particular, this presentation will focus on two main results: first, the development of advanced thermodynamic models to predictively estimate RNA/lipid solubilities and other important physical properties; and second, the application of phase-field models (PFMs) within a multiscale simulation framework to study the anti-solvent precipitation and RNA encapsulation process. Insights gained from the various models are mapped back to product quality attributes and process insights. Lastly, the use of the models to guide development of advanced process control and optimization strategies is discussed.

topic: Virtual High-Throughput Screening of Transition Metal Mechanophores with Ab Initio Modeling and Machine Learning
title: Virtual High-Throughput Screening of Transition Metal Mechanophores with Ab Initio Modeling and Machine Learning
abstract: Mechanophores are force-responsive molecules that undergo controlled bond breaking or rearrangement under applied force. Due to their diverse physical and chemical responses to mechanical stimuli, mechanophores broad applications in polymer strengthening, force probing, drug delivery, and waste polymer applications and have been extensively studied in recent years. Neverhtless, the majority of existing mechanophores are organic molecules, and mechanophore design and discovery currently relies on less efficient experimental trial-and-error. Expansion of mechanophore space to transition metal containing mechanophores would allow for even greater tunability of properties, but their synthesis and experimental characterization is more challenging than their organic counterparts. We have thus implemented a workflow for high-throughput computational discovery of transition metal mechanophores. First, we screen the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) to gather synthetically accessible molecular candidates for two classes of mechanophores: spin-crossover and coordination-switching. Across more than 1,100 candidate complexes, we carry out force-free geometry optimizations using density functional theory (DFT), and we also characterize the force-responsiveness of these mechanophores using simulations that explicitly incorporate external force (i.e., EFEI and CoGEF). From these simulations, we identify key chemical features and construct mechanochemistry-tailored machine learning (ML) models to drastically accelerate computational discovery. To date, we have identified 500+ metal mechanophores with high reactivity, distinct and critical functionalities, and versatile for real-world applications. The 150+ spin-crossover mechanophores, for instance, exhibit force-activated spin-crossover between magnetic states. They are thus compatible for in-situ force-probing and damage detection for the majority of engineering polymers which are opaque, resolving the limitations of current mechanophores which rely on optical signals. The 350+ coordination-switching mechanophores, on the other hand, have mechanochemical reactivity comparable with the most labile mechanophores currently discovered. Their facile responses make them building blocks for ultra-strong polymer networks. Finally, we further identified most promising candidates for follow-up synthesis.

topic: Synthesis of Unilammellar Liposomes for Drug Delivery Using Colloidal Packed Bed
title: Synthesis of Unilammellar Liposomes for Drug Delivery Using Colloidal Packed Bed
abstract: Liposome-based drug delivery systems synthesized using colloidal packed bed technology represent a promising advancement in targeted and efficient therapeutic delivery. We highlight the synthesis and application of liposomes through colloidal packed beds, with particular emphasis on their potential for DNA and RNA delivery as well as the treatment of iron deficiency anemia. The colloidal packed bed uses alumina oxide as packing material within an alumina cylindrical tube sintered at 1100 ºC for 30 minutes. Our synthesis process used one-step drying and hydration of lipid films in the packed bed to form desirable small unilamellar liposomes. Additionally, we can obtain low polydisperse liposomes and load cargoes such as iron and DNA. We also aim to achieve higher encapsulation efficiency of iron using anionic lipids such as 1,2-Dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol, sodium salt (DPPG), and DNA using the cationic lipid 1,2-Dioleoyl-3-trimethylammonium propane (DOTAP), as well as the helper lipid 1,2-di-(9Z-octadecenoyl)-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE) and PEGylated lipid (ALC-0159). We aim to adapt our method to accommodate various nucleic acids, including RNA and siRNA, for downstream applications. Synthesized liposomes were measured for size using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS), while the bilayer lamellarity was confirmed using a Cryo-Transmission Electron Microscope (Cryo-TEM). The encapsulation technique using a colloidal packed bed aims to provide an alternative to existing techniques, such as microfluidics and the impinging jet mixer, which are currently used for the synthesis of liposome-based drug delivery systems.

topic: Machine Learning-Enabled Self-Driving Laboratory for Accelerated Emulsifiable Concentrates Design
title: Machine Learning-Enabled Self-Driving Laboratory for Accelerated Emulsifiable Concentrates Design
abstract: Crop protection formulations are essential for improving crop yields to sustain a growing population. However, formulation design and development remain primarily empirical, often requiring up to a year to design a formulation product. While principal rules and empirical methods such as the hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) theory, are effective in control experiments, they struggle to investigate optimal candidate materials for industrial applications. Hence, the development of agrochemical formulation heavily relies on an extensive number of experiments. To accelerate the formulation design process, we will present our level-4 self-driving laboratory (SDL) system for formulation development, powered by machine learning models based on past experimental data. As a level-4 SDL, chemists will design the search space and the SDL will conduct closed-loop experiments which are formed by multiple tasks. This system autonomously designs, conducts, characterises, and refines experiments iteratively. By significantly reducing the workload of formulation scientists, our SDL enhances efficiency and accelerates innovation in crop protection formulation.

topic: Transfer Learning from Batch to Continuous Line for Pharmaceutical Tablet Production
title: Transfer Learning from Batch to Continuous Line for Pharmaceutical Tablet Production
abstract: In the pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturing site, scale, and equipment for a drug product can be changed in the development and commercial production stages, considering the change in demand for clinical trial materials and commercial products. During the early phase of these changes, experimental data are scarce in the new condition, which makes it challenging to build a reliable model using conventional machine learning (ML) approaches. An effective ML technique to tackle the situation with limited data is transfer learning (TL). TL can improve the prediction performance of a model for one domain, i.e., target domain (TD), by transferring knowledge from a related domain, i.e., source domain (SD). Previous research successfully applied TL to pharmaceutical manufacturing process scale-up for roller compaction [1], spray-drying [2], and tableting [3]. However, further investigations are still needed to stimulate TL implementation in the pharmaceutical industry. For example, TL’s applicability has yet to be investigated when a production line with several unit processes is changed to a new one with different unit processes. No previous research has revealed the impact of input variables, including process parameters (PP) and material attributes (MA) of intermediate products, on the TL model’s prediction accuracy for critical quality attributes (CQA). This study aims to clarify TL’s applicability to the transition of a pharmaceutical tablet production line from batch to continuous and evaluate the effect of PP and MA as input variables on CQA prediction accuracy, comparing TL with two conventional ML approaches. This study adopted frustratingly easy heterogeneous domain adaption (FEHDA) [4] as a TL algorithm. FEHDA creates three feature spaces from input variables: 1) common to both SD and TD, 2) unique to SD, and 3) unique to TD. One conventional ML approach is ‘SD+TD’ where a model is constructed using input variables common to SD and TD. The other is ‘TD’ where only TD data are available for model-building. A schematic diagram in the attached image illustrates the matrix structure differences between the three model-building methods. The batch line (BL) and continuous line (CL) were regarded as SD and TD, respectively. BL involves high-shear wet granulation, fluidized bed drying, screening, lubrication blending, and tableting. On the other hand, CL consists of twin screw wet granulation, fluidized bed drying, screening, lubrication blending, and tableting. Since the screening and tableting equipment in BL and CL has the same design and operating principles, the PP of two processes were regarded as input variables common to both domains. In contrast, the PP of the remaining processes in BL and CL were regarded as input variables unique to SD and TD, respectively. MA and lubricant ratio were regarded as input variables common to both domains because they were measured using the same method. The dissolution rate at 15 min (%), a CQA of the final product, was measured as an output variable. Fifteen BL lots and five CL lots were prepared as SD and TD training data to build Gaussian process regression (GPR) [5] models. The GPR model’s prediction performance was evaluated using TD test data of eleven CL lots, which was not included in TD training data. Six GPR models were constructed using two types of input variables, i.e., PP and PP+MA, and three kinds of model-building methods, i.e., TL, SD+TD, and TD. Besides, six TD training/test data combinations were prepared to evaluate the GPR model’s robustness by root mean square error of prediction (RMSEP). A bar chart in the attached image shows the mean and standard deviation values of RMSEP for the six GPR models. When using only PP as input variables, the TL model achieved the smallest RMSEP value of 3.6%, compared to the RMSEP values of 5.1% and 5.8% in the SD+TD and TD models, respectively. While the SD+TD model used only PP that are common to both domains, the TL model employed not only PP common to both domains but also PP unique to each domain, which contributed to improving the prediction performance of the TL model. In addition, the TL model with only PP achieved the RMSEP value of 3.6% without using MA as input variables, which was comparable to the RMSEP values of 3.5% and 3.3% in the TL and SD+TD models with PP+MA. Using MA as input variables common to both domains improved the RMSEP value of the SD+TD model, because MA potentially correlate with CQA, and their relationship is independent of manufacturing equipment. Regardless of input variable types, the TD models were not robust and showed the worst RMSEP values due to the scarcity of TD training data. This study concludes that TL can improve prediction accuracy even when MA data are not available. Consequently, TL holds the potential to streamline process development activities by reducing the time and cost required for MA data collection. Furthermore, a PP-based TL model could be critical in CQA prediction when intermediate products such as powders and granules cannot be sampled in the containment facilities for highly potent APIs, or manufacturing site is transferred to a contract manufacturing organization. topic: Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning for Designing Peptide Probes for Vapor-Phase Sensing to Improve Disease Diagnostics and Monitoring.
title: Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning for Designing Peptide Probes for Vapor-Phase Sensing to Improve Disease Diagnostics and Monitoring.
abstract: Rapid and non-invasive tests for disease can be crucial for human health, especially during pandemics like COVID-19. Breath analysis hold promise as an approach for disease detection, as the human breath contains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that vary in balance with the illness. Traditional disease diagnostic tools are often slow, invasive or require travel to a testing site. A preliminary study has validated the concept of developing a biosensor comprising a multiplex of peptide probes capable of binding diseased VOCs for diagnosing diseases. These peptides, ranging from 8 to 20 amino acids, inherit molecular motifs and VOC-binding affinities akin to odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), with additional features for easy immobilization on a transistor surface. The study has demonstrated selective electrical response to a target VOC verses a confounding VOC in a simulated breath flow. However, homology transfer is not flawless, and eliminating binding residues from their native protein structure alters their conformational behavior and exact VOC-binding profile. Methods are needed to fine-tune the sequence of each peptide probe in the sensor design to enhance the specificity of the entire multiplex for targeting diseases. In this project, we aim to develop and verify a high-throughput computational screen for peptide/VOC binding: The project aims to create a physics-based computational screen using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and enhanced sampling methods, such as Metadynamics (MetaD) to predict the binding affinities between peptide probes and VOC molecules. This screen will allow for the exploration of many potential peptide sequences and generate data points for machine learning (ML) modeling. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will be used both for developing new fundamental understanding (e.g., structure function relationships in peptide/VOC bound states) while also providing key information for training ML models to estimate binding affinity from sequence alone.

topic: Novel Ligand Discovery for Rare Earth Element Separation Using Chemical Language Model and High-Throughput Experiments
title: Novel Ligand Discovery for Rare Earth Element Separation Using Chemical Language Model and High-Throughput Experiments
abstract: Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are indispensable to modern technologies, including renewable energy, electronics, defense systems, and advanced medical devices. Despite their importance, REE supply chains remain vulnerable to geopolitical tensions and environmental challenges. Additionally, separating individual REEs is difficult due to their similar physicochemical properties and their co-occurrence in deposits. Liquid–liquid extraction (LLE), relying on ligand-metal binding affinity, is the primary industrial method for REE recovery. However, current LLE ligand extractants typically have low binding affinity and separation efficiency towards REE, requiring extensive solvent usage and generating significant waste. Therefore, developing innovative extraction technologies, especially novel ligands with enhanced binding affinity and selectivity towards REEs is essential. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have shown promise in predicting ligands for REEs but still face key limitations. The lack of publicly available datasets and limited experimental data hinder the development and validation of robust predictive models. Furthermore, existing methods largely focus on prediction rather than ligand design, underscoring the need for innovative approaches capable of designing novel and effective molecules for REE separations. Recently, large language models (LLMs), specifically chemical language models (CLMs), have revolutionized novel molecule design. Pre-trained on billions of molecules, CLMs serve as a powerful framework to enhance the performance of downstream tasks in situations with limited labeled data, paving the way for breakthroughs in REE binding ligands design. In this work, we aim to leverage state-of-the-art AI and ML methods combined with high-throughput experimental techniques to design novel ligands for efficient REE separation. Summarizing data from previous literature, we first fine-tuned pre-trained CLMs to obtain a ligand-REE binding affinity predictor. We then applied this trained predictor to screen a large molecule set and identify novel ligands with potentially enhanced REE binding affinity. These candidate ligands underwent high-throughput experimental validation, significantly increasing available experimental data. This newly validated data was reincorporated into the training dataset, enhancing model accuracy and extrapolative capabilities through an active learning cycle. This iterative cycle of prediction, validation, and refinement continuously improved model performance, ultimately producing a robust REE-binding affinity predictor and facilitating the discovery of novel ligands with superior binding affinity and selectivity.

topic: Similarity-Based Classification of Concentration Profiles in Chemical Reactions to Assist Kinetic Model Development
title: Similarity-Based Classification of Concentration Profiles in Chemical Reactions to Assist Kinetic Model Development
abstract: In the fields of reaction engineering and process systems engineering, the development of mechanistic models based on physical and chemical principles has long been a central focus. Within the domain of organic chemistry, kinetic studies play a crucial role in bridging the understanding of reaction mechanisms with the construction of predictive models. Despite their value, the application of kinetic approaches in organic synthesis has historically been limited [1]. This is largely due to the deep domain knowledge and significant manual effort required to analyze and interpret reaction mechanisms for model development. Since around 2005, however, there has been a noticeable increase in research dedicated to kinetic studies of organic reactions [2–5]. In addition, new analytical methodologies have emerged—such as reaction progress kinetic analysis [1, 5, 6] and variable time normalization analysis [7, 8]—which have improved the accessibility of kinetic evaluation. More recently, efforts have been made to incorporate machine learning techniques into kinetic analysis workflows. These include platforms like AI-DARWIN [9] and studies on classifying organic reaction mechanisms using machine learning [10]. Nevertheless, previous studies have primarily focused on specific types of reactions, which limits their general applicability across a broader range of chemical systems. In this study, we propose a data-driven framework that enables automatic classification of chemical reactions based on their time-dependent concentration profiles, thereby facilitating the identification of underlying mechanisms and the construction of corresponding kinetic models. Our approach focuses on extracting similarity among various reactions by comparing their normalized concentration-time data. By identifying the most similar cases from a reference dataset, we aim to identify possible mechanisms and rate laws that govern the unknown reaction under investigation. We confirmed that neural network-based models can effectively capture nonlinear and dynamic features of the reaction profiles. In addition, several similarity evaluation methods will be explored, such as k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN). Once a similar reaction is identified, the system suggests potential kinetic model candidates and fits the model parameters to the observed data. This could enable automatic selection and construction of the most appropriate kinetic representation for the given reaction. [1] D. G.
