topic: AI-Powered Materials Discovery and Design: A Computational Framework for Tailoring Microstructural Properties
title: AI-Powered Materials Discovery and Design: A Computational Framework for Tailoring Microstructural Properties
abstract: Inverse design remains a central challenge in materials engineering, where optimizing microstructures to achieve targeted properties is often computationally prohibitive. Traditional methods struggle with inverting structure-property relationships due to the high dimensionality and stochastic complexity of microstructures. To overcome these challenges, we introduce PoreFlow , a data-driven computational framework that leverages continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) for high-throughput microstructure generation. Unlike conventional generative models, PoreFlow embeds target properties directly into the latent space, enabling precise and efficient inverse design. We demonstrate the power of this approach through the generation of 3D porous microstructures, where our model consistently achieves R2 scores above 91.5% for reconstruction and greater than 92% for new sample generation. Compared to GAN-based models, which often face instability and mode collapse, PoreFlow offers a robust, stable training process and enhanced interpretability. Its modular architecture also allows for extensions beyond image-based design representations by modifying the autoencoder component. This work has broad implications for materials discovery and design in various applications such as energy storage, catalysis, and beyond, providing a scalable and interpretable method for engineering microstructures with tailored properties. By integrating machine learning and materials informatics, PoreFlow advances inverse design, making it faster, more reliable, and more accessible to researchers and engineers.

topic: Data-Driven Spray Deposition of Self-Assembled Block Copolymer Thin Films: A Scalable Approach for Morphology Control and Mechanistic Insights
title: Data-Driven Spray Deposition of Self-Assembled Block Copolymer Thin Films: A Scalable Approach for Morphology Control and Mechanistic Insights
abstract: Block copolymer (BCP) thin films are useful for synthesizing functional materials because of their well-known capabilities to self-assemble into organized nanoscale structures. These materials can be utilized in diverse applications, including lithographic nanopatterning, nanoporous membrane fabrication, and nano-catalysis. However, for their widespread implementation there is need for precise control over their nanoscale morphology using scalable and cost-effective deposition methods. Current synthesis approaches usually involve multi-step processes, specialized materials, and equipment, limiting scalability while increasing costs. Spray deposition techniques address these limitations by enabling the coating of non-planar substrates and reducing manufacturing complexity and costs. In this study, we present a data-driven scalable spray-deposition method to fabricate self-assembled, nanostructured thin films with tailored morphologies. By integrating machine learning algorithms, we optimize the precursor composition and spray parameters to achieve well-defined morphologies directly during deposition in a single step, eliminating the need for post-deposition annealing. Using a program-controlled ultrasonic spray system we explored the complex phase map of six poly(styrene-block-2-vinylpyridine) (PS-b-P2VP) diblock copolymer systems, which are deposited onto functionalized silicon wafers. This simple process yielded various nanostructures, including horizontal cylinders, vertical inverse cylinders, vertical lamellae, and hybrid structures. Also, we monitored the structure formation during the drying process using GISAXS and spectroscopic ellipsometry and confirmed the final morphologies with SEM imaging. The in-situ characterization allows better understanding of the morphology formation mechanism. This method provides a rapid, cost-effective, and scalable approach for producing morphology-controlled BCP films on a wide range of substrates, map the morphology phase space and provide mechanistic insight on the formation process.

topic: Resonance Invariant Graph Representation (RIGR) for Molecular Property Prediction
title: Resonance Invariant Graph Representation (RIGR) for Molecular Property Prediction
abstract: Chemical datasets predominantly use SMILES strings to represent molecules, which provide a convenient encoding of Lewis structures by depicting atoms and their bonds, such as single and double bonds. Most machine learning software packages for chemistry, such as chemprop, rely on this SMILES representation as their input. However, this representation depicts only a single resonance structure, even for molecules with multiple resonance forms—common in drug design, organic photovoltaics, and agrochemicals. If a different resonance structure is provided as input, the software may interpret it as a different molecule and produce a different prediction. To overcome this problem, we introduce a Resonance Invariant Graph Representation (RIGR). RIGR is a graph featurizer that inherently ensures resonance invariance by using only resonance invariant atom and bond features in chemprop. By mapping all resonance structures of a molecule to a single graph and discarding resonance-dependent features like bond type, RIGR eliminates the ambiguity in molecular representation. We present a detailed comparison of RIGR's performance against chemprop's native featurizer in predicting the standard heat of formation. We introduce metrics to quantify resonance variance and assess its impact on model predictions. Additionally, we perform Shapley analysis to examine the model's reliance on different atom and bond features, revealing that many features of the native featurizer hold limited relevance in making the final prediction. Using 60% fewer features, the models trained with RIGR show consistent feature importance across different weight initializations, requiring a smaller ensemble of models. While augmenting the data with all resonance structures for training offers a solid solution for implicitly imposing resonance invariance, it introduces significant computational challenges and costs. We also quantify the impact of dataset size, demonstrating that RIGR's performance remains robust, even on smaller datasets. For broader use beyond resonance, RIGR achieves comparable results across chemprop benchmarks for both regression and classification tasks. Building on these promising results, we leverage RIGR to develop a robust, chemistry-informed ML model for predicting gas-phase radical thermochemistry, where resonance plays a significant role. Ultimately, RIGR offers a robust featurizer that enforces resonance invariance while maintaining performance on property prediction tasks and avoids the complexities of generating and augmenting resonance structures. RIGR paves the way for the development of interpretable, chemistry-informed machine learning models.

topic: Dimensional Evolution of Physical Force- and Field-Induced Chirality: From 2D Elastomeric Metasurfaces to 3D Magnetoplasmonic Superstructures and Beyond
title: Dimensional Evolution of Physical Force- and Field-Induced Chirality: From 2D Elastomeric Metasurfaces to 3D Magnetoplasmonic Superstructures and Beyond
abstract: The ability to dynamically control chiral optical properties is essential for advancing next-generation optoelectronic and photonic applications. In this study, we demonstrate a dimensional evolution in chirality modulation, transitioning from two-dimensional (2D) elastomeric metasurfaces to three-dimensional (3D) plasmonic chiral responses induced by helical magnetic fields. By integrating these approaches, we establish a unified strategy for achieving real-time and reconfigurable chirality control. We first fabricate fingerprint-inspired elastomeric grating metasurfaces (EGMS) using a nanoimprinting method with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) followed by gold deposition. These metasurfaces exhibit chiral optical responses due to symmetry breaking induced by pattern (P) and curvature (T), which can be actively tuned by adjusting the skew angle (θ). As a 2D chiral system, EGMS provides a robust platform for structural chirality manipulation. Extending this concept into the 3D domain, we explore plasmonic chiral nanostructures influenced by helical magnetic fields. The application of such fields induces a tunable and reversible chiroptical response, enabling precise control over optical activity. This transition from 2D structural chirality to 3D magnetic-field-driven chirality broadens the scope of tunable chiral photonics, demonstrating how external stimuli can dynamically modulate optical properties. By bridging structural and plasmonic chiral modulation across different dimensions, this study establishes a versatile framework for the design of tunable optical filters, sensors, and polarization-dependent devices. The synergy between 2D metasurfaces and 3D magnetic-field-driven chirality provides a new avenue for the development of advanced chiral photonic materials with broad applications in optoelectronics.

topic: Screening of Solvents for Capturing PFAS Via a Data Science Approach
title: Screening of Solvents for Capturing PFAS Via a Data Science Approach
abstract: The development and broad application of single-layer and multilayer (ML) plastics in the food packaging, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics industries have served various purposes, including ensuring consumer product safety, shelf life, and handling (Barry, 2022). However, the recycling rate for these materials is low, particularly in the US, which only reaches 9% (Geyer et al. 2017). The emergence of solvent-based-physical plastic separation processes, such as the Solvent Targeted Recovery And Precipitation (STRAP™) process, has facilitated the recycling of these plastic wastes that cannot be mechanically recycled, resulting in the heightened recyclability of post-industrial waste plastics (Walker et al. 2020; Zhao et al. 2018). This technology involves the sequential separation of ML plastics into their various polymer constituents over a series of solvent washes, recovering high-quality polymer resins for reuse in food packaging and other consumer products. However, with the emergence of the Chemicals of Concern (Aurisano et al. 2021; Zimmermann et al. 2022) such as Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) that may be non-intentionally introduced (Tumu et al. 2024) into post-consumer waste (PCW) plastics somewhere along the plastic waste management supply chain such as the material recovery facilities, human use, or the environment, current mechanical and solvent-based recycling infrastructures face a significant challenge in ensuring contaminant-free recycled plastics. Moreover, the ubiquitousness of PFAS in the environment and their endocrine-disruptive nature has prompted legislative bans on the industrial use of fluorinated compounds as processing aids, including fluoropolymers across the US, particularly in the food packaging industry, to varying detection limits (Bulawska et al. 2025; Norris et al. 2022; Zheng et al. 2023). Therefore, extending solvent-based plastic recycling infrastructures to remediate short-chain PFAS from PCW plastics is paramount for increasing the recyclability of plastic wastes. However, unlike the finite number of polymers, 15,000 EPA-identified small-molecule PFAS could contaminate PCW plastics (Gaines et al. 2023). Therefore, this study applies data science approaches to quickly identify solvents to capture these PFAS from plastic wastes – ensuring PFAS-free post-consumer recycled plastics. This study expands the STRAP process to incorporate the capture of PFAS using solvents by treating them as an additional layer in selective dissolution. The objective is to identify solvents that selectively dissolve PFAS while preserving other polymers present in the PCW plastics. This approach leverages the partition coefficient (LogD) and the solubility of PFAS in various solvents—predicted via molecular-scale modeling—to identify solvents that facilitate the preferential partitioning of PFAS (LogD > 0) from the polymer matrix into the solvent phase. Specifically, the partition coefficients of each PFAS in different polymers and solvents are essential for evaluating a solvent’s ability to extract PFAS from a given polymer. Additionally, the solubility of each PFAS in different solvents must be assessed to determine the effectiveness of each solvent in capturing PFAS. This molecular-scale modeling involves performing density functional theorem (DFT) calculations on each PFAS to obtain their surface screening charges (i.e., sigma profiles) that necessitate the prediction of relevant molecular properties and the use of the COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) software, grounded in quantum chemistry principles, that enables accurate prediction of their LogD and solubilities. However, predicting the LogD of the 15,000 PFAS in 10 different polymers present in PCW plastics in 1000 solvent requires ~15,000,000 molecular simulations or experiments and over 15,000 human hours of simulation time, eliminating the feasibility of experimental screening approaches and requiring significant computational resources. Therefore, PFAS remediation from PCW plastics requires leveraging data science tools for a more efficient PFAS capture strategy. Hypothesizing that structurally similar PFAS have similar molecular properties, this work identifies families of structurally similar PFAS via dimensionality reduction approaches and identifies solvents that can target each family. This approach significantly reduces the number of molecular simulations by 100,000 times and the computational time required. The Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) keys, a one-hot encoding molecular representation, obtained from the open-source rdkit python library, were adopted to represent each PFAS molecule, and t-SNE, a dimensionality reduction technique, was used to transform the structural data from a high-dimensional space to a low-dimensional space for easy visualization. This analysis successfully identified seven distinct families of PFAS having different functional groups and structural features. To test our hypothesis founded on structural similarity, we selected 50 PFAS spanning the entire latent space to perform a pair-wise comparison between their similarity score and LogD magnitude difference. Using polyethylene (PE) as the reference polymer, the LogD values of each PFAS were predicted in five different solvents using the COSMO-RS software. Our results show that 70% similarity is the threshold value for our hypothesis to hold. Therefore, using this threshold value, we performed a guided clustering to determine the number of clusters that would ensure a minimum of 70% structural similarity within each cluster across the entire PFAS latent space. Due to the inherent inability of existing dimensionality techniques, such as t-SNE and UMAP, to perform such guided clustering, a graph-based clustering approach was adopted. Given the 70% threshold value, an undirected graph was developed to represent the interconnectivity between PFAS based on this similarity threshold value (i.e., nodes representing PFAS and edges with at least 70% similarity). While ongoing works involve examining the topology of our undirected graph to identify clusters of interconnected PFAS, our results show that 800 PFAS are structurally unique, having no connection with other PFAS. This result provides insights into PFAS that may be difficult or easy to target via solvent-based approaches. Our results also show that tetrahydrofuran (THF), a biomass-based solvent, proves promising in targeting a wide variety of PFAS from PE. Other ongoing works include applying our solvent screening framework to an existing ML plastic film to identify families of PFAS targeted using selected solvents proposing solvent-based plastic recycling also as a possible pretreatment step for other plastic recycling technologies. topic: Degradation in PEO- B -PCL Films and the Role of Crystalline Morphology
title: Degradation in PEO- B -PCL Films and the Role of Crystalline Morphology
abstract: PEO- b -PCL (polyethylene oxide- b -polycaprolactone) is an amphiphilic block copolymer that has gained a lot of attention for its biomedical applications. These copolymers are somewhat unique in that the T m s of each block are similar. While crystal formation drives phase separation, the crystal development and relative crystallinities impacts their macroscopic properties. Our previous work has shown that film crystallization behavior can be manipulated using typical techniques such as selective solvent casting and thermal history. Interestingly, when using particular selective solvents, the crystal morphology switches from edge-on spherulites to flat-on lamellae. Because these polymers are valued for their degradation and drug release potential, we are investigating these properties as a function of each block's crystallinity and the overall crystal morphology. Here, the erosion and hydrolytic degradation of PEO- b -PCL films in aqueous solution were shown to vary with weight fraction, crystalline content, and morphology indicating the role of both PEO and PCL crystallization on water uptake, dissolution, and chain decomposition. Additionally, environmental factors such as pH and temperature of the aqueous solution were evaluated.

topic: Early-Stage Conceptual Design and Scale-up Analysis of Continuous Flow Electrosynthesis: A Case Study on Ibuprofen Production Via Electrochemical Carboxylation
title: Early-Stage Conceptual Design and Scale-up Analysis of Continuous Flow Electrosynthesis: A Case Study on Ibuprofen Production Via Electrochemical Carboxylation
abstract: Electrochemical synthesis is emerging as a promising pathway for sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing, offering a greener alternative to traditional chemical routes. While most electrochemical reactions are developed in batch mode, there is growing interest in translating them into continuous flow systems, which offer advantages such as improved control of reaction conditions, enhanced safety, greater productivity, and easier scalability for industrial implementation. However, early-stage design and scale-up of such systems remain underexplored, particularly for pharmaceutical applications. This study presents a structured framework for the conceptual design and scale-up analysis of continuous flow electrosynthesis processes. The framework integrates scale-up modeling, sensitivity analysis, and simulation-based optimization under uncertainty to support informed early-stage decision-making. To demonstrate the framework's applicability, we apply it to the continuous production of ibuprofen via electrochemical carboxylation, adapting the batch process developed by Mena et al. (2019). In this reaction, 1-chloro-4-isobutylbenzene undergoes carboxylation using CO₂ at a silver cathode in ionic liquids. We model the electrochemical reactor as a steady-state plug flow reactor (PFR) with uniform mass transfer characteristics. To represent industrial stack designs, we implement multiple PFRs in parallel, with each PFR representing a single electrolyte flow channel. It is assumed that these channels are positioned between cathode and anode pairs and are separated by membranes to prevent product crossover. Reactor sizing is guided by commercially available electrode surface areas and standard stack configurations to ensure practical feasibility. Additionally, we model post-electrolysis separation and purification steps to enable full-process analysis. The analysis applies the e-NRTL thermodynamic model to account for electrolyte non-idealities. In alignment with the batch experiments, CO₂ is assumed to be pre-dissolved into the electrolyte before entering the reactor, which justifies treating the system as a single-phase liquid process during electrolysis. We conduct a global sensitivity analysis using the Sobol method to identify the most influential input parameters affecting the performance of the process. These include current density, Faradaic efficiency, flow rate, active electrode area, and electrode spacing, all of which influence conversion, energy consumption, and cost. Although Mena et al. report fixed values for current density and Faradaic efficiency, we allow them to vary within realistic engineering ranges to reflect performance variability during scale-up. We incorporate the most impactful parameters as sources of uncertainty into a simulation-based optimization framework proposed by Al et al. (2020). This framework enables efficient evaluation of robust reactor designs and operating strategies that balance process efficiency, utility demand, and economic performance under uncertain conditions. Preliminary results suggest that continuous operation can deliver promising conversion and energy efficiency under moderate current densities. The case study reveals trade-offs between electrochemical performance and overall cost, reinforcing the value of early-stage modeling for practical design decisions. In future work, we will conduct a comparative analysis between this continuous electrochemical process and the chemical multi-step ibuprofen synthesis route. This comparison will focus on energy use, sustainability metrics, and overall process economics. Our findings aim to support the broader transition toward electrified, modular, and sustainable pharmaceutical production systems. References Mena, S., Sanchez, J., & Guirado, G. (2019). abstract: Caffeine and theophylline are bioactive compounds that can be used as scaffolds to synthesize imidazolium salts that serve as precursors to N-heterocyclic thione (NHT) and selone (NHSe) ligands. These chalcogenone ligands have been used to prepare coordination complexes with a variety of metals, including palladium, platinum, silver, and mercury. In particular, the silver compounds have potential applications as anticancer drugs. This presentation outlines the syntheses, molecular structures, reactivity and DFT calculations of four new N-heterocyclic chalcogenone ligands derived from caffeine or theophylline. More specifically, these novel ligands have been used to prepare several series of silver(I) complexes of general formula [Ag((i)CaffE R ) n ]X (n = 2, 3, 4; R = Me, Bz; E = S, Se; X = NO 3 , BF 4 , ClO 4 ), several of which have been structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography. In order to assess the electronic effect of the pyrimidinedione backbone in the caffeine derivatives, the simpler imidazole-based analogues and their silver complexes have also been isolated and fully characterized. Experimental and computational studies to evaluate and correlate the biological activity of the silver complexes will also be discussed in this presentation.

topic: AI-Driven End-to-End Digital Twins for Pharmaceutical Process Development
title: AI-Driven End-to-End Digital Twins for Pharmaceutical Process Development
abstract: Digital twins are increasingly recognised as valuable tools in pharmaceutical process development, offering virtual models that support design, control, and optimisation. However, their adoption remains challenging, not only due to the technical complexity but also because developing comprehensive end-to-end process models has traditionally required expertise spanning multiple disciplines. Historically, a team of specialists was necessary to navigate process interdependencies and extract meaningful insights. In this presentation, we explore how AI-driven workflows can help bridge these gaps, empowering individuals to construct and interpret end-to-end digital twins with greater confidence. By guiding users past common blockers—such as selecting an appropriate modelling approach when data is sparse—our framework facilitates the integration of mechanistic, hybrid, and data-driven models. We illustrate this through case studies demonstrating how AI-driven agents suggest structured modelling workflows grounded in process systems engineering principles. These workflows serve as stepwise guides, enabling scientists to progress systematically from experimentation to model-based insights. Beyond the technical aspects, we discuss the regulatory and practical challenges that must be addressed to integrate these digital twins into pharmaceutical development. By lowering the barriers to process modelling, we aim to provide a framework that enhances accessibility, enabling broader adoption of AI-driven digital twins and ultimately supporting more efficient, insight-driven drug development.

topic: Experimental and Theoretical Studies of an Aminosilane As Inhibitor to Achieve Area-Selective Deposition of HfO 2 on SiO 2
title: Experimental and Theoretical Studies of an Aminosilane As Inhibitor to Achieve Area-Selective Deposition of HfO 2 on SiO 2
abstract: The ongoing miniaturization of semiconductor devices drives the development of efficient and robust device manufacturing techniques. Current device fabrication integrates a wide range of nanomaterials via time-consuming, top-down patterning approaches involving hundreds of deposition, lithography, etch, and stripping steps. Area selective deposition is a promising bottom-up technique that directly deposits a patterned layer through surface treatment. Amongst vapor phase deposition techniques, atomic layer deposition (ALD) harnesses self-limiting surface chemistries to deposit uniform, pinhole-free, conformal thin films over high-aspect ratio structures. Area-selective atomic layer deposition engages the advantages of both to achieve selective deposition with precise control over film thickness and properties. Typically, inhibitors such as self-assembled monolayers and small molecule inhibitors are used to facilitate selective growth on one surface over another. However, their carbonaceous groups may lead to undesired carbon contamination and thereby compromised device performance. This study uses experimental and computational methods to explore bisdiethylaminosilane (BDEAS) as an inhibitor against HfO 2 ALD on a native SiO 2 surface. BDEAS forms a carbon-free –SiH 2 terminated inhibition layer via bidentate chemisorption to surface hydroxyl groups, which otherwise would serve as ALD active sites. Density functional theory (DFT) modeling demonstrates inherent selectivity of BDEAS adsorption on hydroxyl- rather than amine-terminated surfaces. Key process parameters are identified from first principles, and corresponding process controls — vapor pressure, dosing time, and soaking time — are tuned to identify the optimal inhibitor deposition regime. The blocking ability of BDEAS is quantified experimentally and compared with that of di-isopropylaminosilane (DIPAS), an inhibitor which forms –SiH 3 terminations. Compared to DIPAS, the blocking ability of BDEAS is limited because of less favorable polydentate chemisorption energetics and steric hinderance from its dual reactive groups. Experimental results indicate that BDEAS has less blocking ability than DIPAS due to the degradation of the inhibition layer with hafnium precursor pulses. Theoretical calculations of energetics along the reaction coordinate reveal key differences in reaction mechanisms and resulting surface terminations of the two inhibitors, shedding light on their respective inhibitor layer degradation mechanisms. Post-deposition annealing targeted at improving resistance of the inhibition layer to precursor-induced degradation improves BDEAS blocking ability as confirmed experimentally. DFT modeling show changes in reaction energetics arising from the anneal which explain the blocking ability differences. Overall, this study demonstrates the impact of denticity and ligand size in determining inhibitor blocking ability and showcases how effective choices of inhibitor molecule, post-deposition processing, and ALD process work synergistically to achieve selectivity and enable bottom-up integration of nanomaterials for device fabrication.

topic: Protein Language-Based Model for Cell-Penetrating Biopolymers in Multi- Cargo Intracellular Delivery
title: Protein Language-Based Model for Cell-Penetrating Biopolymers in Multi- Cargo Intracellular Delivery
abstract: Biopolymers are promising candidates for therapeutic applications in diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. Among them, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) facilitate the intracellular delivery of therapeutic and diagnostic cargo, including small molecules, proteins, and oligonucleotides. While machine learning (ML) approaches have proven effective in predicting CPPs using sequence-based features, existing methods often rely on a limited set of handcrafted descriptors. Recent advances in transformers and large language models (LLMs) suggest that self-supervised learning can extract more informative sequence features, surpassing traditional feature engineering in predictive performance. Our study develops a protein language model-based approach to design and analyze CPPs for delivering small peptides (5–10 amino acids) as cargo inside cells. We leverage pretrained protein language models (ESM variants, BEPLER, and ProtBERT) to generate sequence embeddings, which are fed into a deep learning model using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for binary classification of CPPs. Unlike conventional approaches, our model considers CPP sequences with and without cargo as distinct inputs, enabling predictions of whether a given CPP remains functional after cargo loading. To complement our ML-based predictions, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to investigate CPP-membrane interactions, providing deeper insights into their biophysical properties. In summary, our study integrates machine learning and MD simulations to advance the understanding and design of CPPs, with potential applications in drug delivery, gene therapy, and precision medicine, where efficient intracellular transport of biomolecules remains a significant challenge.

topic: Dissecting Cr-Doped Interfaces: How Diffusion Dynamics Reshape the Van Der Waals Gap and Shift Sb₂Te₃ Thermoelectric Performance
title: Dissecting Cr-Doped Interfaces: How Diffusion Dynamics Reshape the Van Der Waals Gap and Shift Sb₂Te₃ Thermoelectric Performance
abstract: The development of advanced thermoelectric materials is crucial for sustainable energy conversion and efficient waste heat recovery. Among promising candidates, Sb₂Te₃ is recognized for its exceptional thermoelectric performance near room temperature and its classification as a topological insulator, offering potential for spintronic and quantum computing applications. However, the structural and electronic effects induced by doping, particularly transition metals such as chromium (Cr), are not fully understood, especially concerning the critical role of the intrinsic van der Waals (vdW) gap. In this study, we employ an integrated approach combining density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations, machine learning (ML) techniques, and experimental validations to systematically investigate how Cr doping influences the structural, electronic, and thermoelectric properties of Sb₂Te₃. Benchmarking studies confirm the necessity of incorporating van der Waals corrections and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) for accurately modeling these systems, which possess significant relativistic and layered interactions. We find that Cr atoms preferentially occupy substitutional sites rather than interstitial positions within the lattice, significantly altering the thermodynamic stability and the vdW gap. Detailed analysis of Cr migration pathways reveals that diffusion mechanisms and migration barriers are critically dependent on the vdW gap dimensions, creating a complex interplay that dictates the final doping configuration and stability. Our results indicate that vdW gap modulation induced by Cr doping leads to substantial structural changes and significant shifts in electronic band structure, notably influencing the positions of Dirac points at the Γ and A points. Manual adjustments of the vdW gap distance in pristine Sb₂Te₃, independent of Cr doping, further underscore the direct relationship between vdW gap alterations and electronic bandstructure transformations. To disentangle the mechanical and magnetic effects of Cr, we conducted additional simulations removing Cr atoms post-relaxation. These simulations confirm that structural modifications in the vdW gap alone substantially affect electronic behavior, highlighting the vdW gap as a central descriptor influencing electronic properties. AIMD simulations conducted at room temperature reveal dynamic evolution of vdW gaps, emphasizing their stability and sensitivity to realistic operating conditions. Additionally, simulations under external pressure demonstrate the mechanical robustness of the Cr-doped system and provide insights into alternative strategies for vdW gap tuning beyond chemical doping. Using BoltzTraP2 calculations, we quantify the impact of Cr doping on thermal transport properties, revealing that variations in vdW gap distances significantly enhance phonon scattering, particularly in the low-frequency regime. This leads to reductions in lattice thermal conductivity and improvements in thermoelectric performance. Consequently, we propose that the vdW gap dimension can serve as a potent, tunable parameter to optimize thermoelectric materials. Ultimately, this comprehensive study provides a novel framework integrating computational modeling, machine learning-driven design, and experimental validation, establishing a closed-loop, autonomous approach for materials discovery. Our findings position the vdW gap as a critical, predictive descriptor within machine learning models, facilitating the targeted design of multifunctional thermoelectric and spintronic materials.

topic: Thermal Conversion of Cotton Gin Byproducts into Liquid Fuels and High-Value Chemicals
title: Thermal Conversion of Cotton Gin Byproducts into Liquid Fuels and High-Value Chemicals
abstract: Cotton Gin Byproducts (CGB) have become a major challenge for the cotton ginning industry over the years due to the large volume of material produced annually, leading to issues associated with their handling and proper disposal. CGB are composed mainly of cotton burrs, motes, sticks, leaf parts, and fine woody particles, which are generated by various equipment in the ginning process, mainly during seed cotton and lint cleaning. Studies on CGB suggest that they have significant potential as a biofuel feedstock due to their cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin composition, like other widely studied agricultural residues such as rice straw, wheat straw, etc. Thermochemical methods of conversion have emerged as promising approaches to convert biomass into liquid fuels for (bio)energy applications, including upgrades for use as transportation fuel. However, the potential of these thermochemical processes for efficiently converting CGB into biofuels remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the potential of converting CGB into liquid fuel and high-value chemicals through three thermochemical processes: fast pyrolysis, catalytic pyrolysis, and hydropyrolysis. Five CGB samples were collected from equipment at different stages of the ginning process (cylinder cleaners, stick machine, and the “trash master”) at the USDA-ARS micro-gin in Stoneville, MS. Preliminary proximate analysis revealed an average volatile matter of 69 wt.%, 7.3 wt.% fixed carbon, 10 wt.% moisture content, and ash content of 10 wt.% across the five CGB samples. The average carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulfur, and oxygen contents were found to be 43.5%, 4.7%, 2.8%, 0.4%, and 37.5 wt.%, respectively. The higher heating value ranged from 15 to 17 MJ/kg. In this work, we initially subject the CGB samples to fast pyrolysis in a CDS Analytical Pyroprobe at a temperature of 500°C, and the resulting pyrolysis vapors are analyzed using Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry/Flame Ionization Detector (GC-MS/FID) to determine their chemical composition and product distribution. We also investigate the effect of catalytic pyrolysis using conventional HZSM-5 and a modified zeolite catalyst (2D-nanosheets) to enhance the selectivity to aromatic compounds while minimizing undesired oxygenated compounds. The samples will also be converted in the presence of hydrogen (hydropyrolysis) to assess the effect of hydrogenation of the pyrolysis products into aromatics and cycloalkanes. Previous studies have demonstrated that hydropyrolysis and the use of metal-doped zeolites improve the degree of deoxygenation and promote the formation of aromatics such as benzene, toluene, and xylenes (BTX), which are critical intermediates for fuel applications. We hypothesize that the variability in the composition of the CGB from the different stages in the ginning process will result in distinct product distributions, and that modified 2D nanosheet zeolites will outperform conventional HZSM-5 catalysts in increasing the yield of aromatic hydrocarbons. Furthermore, we expect hydropyrolysis to produce higher hydrocarbon yields by reducing oxygenates through hydrodeoxygenation. We are confident our findings will contribute to the development of improved thermochemical processes for converting cotton gin byproducts into liquid fuels and high-value chemicals, which can serve to reduce the abundance of this agricultural byproduct, provide transportation liquid fuels, and ultimately advance sustainable fuel production.

topic: Optimizing La/Sr Ratio in La y Sr 1-Y Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 Perovskites for Enhanced Catalytic Performance in Dry Reforming of Methane
title: Optimizing La/Sr Ratio in La y Sr 1-Y Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 Perovskites for Enhanced Catalytic Performance in Dry Reforming of Methane
abstract: Enhancing catalyst stability and efficiency in dry reforming of methane (DRM) is essential for syngas production, requiring materials with high activity and resistance to carbon deposition. This study explores the impact of Sr substitution for La in La y Sr 1-y Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 perovskites, emphasizing their structural integrity, oxygen mobility, and catalytic properties. XRD analysis confirms the formation of well-crystallized perovskites, while TPR and XPS reveal that Sr incorporation increases oxygen vacancies, stabilizing the lattice and shifting Ni reduction to higher temperatures. The La-rich composition (y = 1) demonstrates the highest catalytic activity, reaching 88% CO 2 and 75% CH 4 conversion at 750 °C. Conversely, the Sr-rich sample (y = 0) shows enhanced oxygen vacancy formation and basicity but lower catalytic efficiency, with 27% CO 2 and 20% CH 4 conversion at 500 °C, due to SrCO 3 formation reducing active site availability. The interaction between La and Sr plays a crucial role in tuning Ni reducibility, where La promotes Ni reduction, while Sr delays low-temperature reduction. La 0.5 Sr 0.5 Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 achieves an optimal balance of oxygen mobility and catalytic performance, effectively minimizing coke formation. The incorporation of Mg further enhances stability and CO 2 adsorption. However, excessive La content increases carbon deposition, emphasizing the need for a carefully adjusted La/Sr ratio. These findings highlight the significance of La/Sr composition in optimizing perovskite catalysts for DRM, providing valuable insights into their structural and catalytic properties for efficient syngas production. topic: Assessing the Impact of Biomass Burning on Air Quality in West Bengal
title: Assessing the Impact of Biomass Burning on Air Quality in West Bengal
abstract: Biomass burning is widely believed to be a contributor to poor air quality in Indo Gangetic Plain (IGP) region in India, but its contribution within the state of West Bengal is not well recognized. This is partly due to the dominance of other pollution sources in the region and differences in harvest schedules compared to other parts of the IGP. This study integrates remote sensing data along with ground-level PM2.5 measurements in an attempt to establish a data-driven association between biomass burning and air quality across multiple districts in West Bengal. Remote sensing data is used to capture fire activity across the state along with data on trace gases concentrations. A network of over 220 low-cost sensors is used to obtain ground based PM2.5 measurements across the state at high spatio-temporal resolution. By aligning weekly fire activity with district-level PM2.5 data, we perform a spatiotemporal analysis to quantify the impact of biomass burning on PM2.5 concentration across the state. The concentrations of co-emitted trace gases such as CO, NO₂, SO 2 , NH 4 derived from remote sensing data is also incorporated into the analysis to isolate biomass burning from other contributors. Correlation analyses are conducted to evaluate the statistical association between fire activity and PM2.5 concentrations. Preliminary results show a strong correlation between fire incidents and localized PM2.5 surges, particularly during peak burning periods in some districts. While this observation holds true for certain agricultural areas, other districts show a relatively weaker association, suggesting that crop burning may play a lesser role in those regions. The effect of cross-state transport and regional contribution is also studies in this work. These findings provide a more quantitative understanding of biomass burning’s role in overall air quality across the state of West Bengal.

topic: Small Angle x-Ray Scattering (SAXS) Analysis of Modified PNA for Autosense
title: Small Angle x-Ray Scattering (SAXS) Analysis of Modified PNA for Autosense
abstract: Peptide nucleic acid (PNA) is applicable as autosense for targeting complementary RNA or DNA. It has the advantages of high stability and efficacy yet suffers from low solubility. Here, we report a small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analysis on the aggregation behavior and conformation of a series of PNA modified systems, which can target specific RNA. The morphology and autosense efficiency of modified PNAs are drastically different and seemingly strongly correlated. We will demonstrate SAXS can be a powerful tool to identify nanoscale morphology and determine the aggregation behavior.

topic: Trust Region Bayesian Optimization with Tanimoto Similarity for Efficient, Scalable, and Progressive Molecular Design
title: Trust Region Bayesian Optimization with Tanimoto Similarity for Efficient, Scalable, and Progressive Molecular Design
abstract: Molecular property optimization (MPO) – the task of identifying molecules with desirable physicochemical or functional properties – is central to fields such as drug discovery, materials design, and catalysis [1]. MPO problems are notoriously difficult: molecular spaces are discrete, structured, and high-dimensional, and property evaluations (e.g., quantum mechanical calculations or experimental synthesis) are typically expensive. Traditional optimization methods struggle in these settings due to limited sample efficiency and an inability to handle complex chemical structure-property relationships [2]. Bayesian optimization (BO) [3] provides a promising framework for such problems, as it is explicitly designed to be sample-efficient in black-box settings. However, standard BO methods often assume continuous design spaces and can fail when applied to molecular domains. They may propose structurally unrealistic candidates, make large and experimentally infeasible jumps across chemical space, or depend on representations that do not respect chemical validity. These limitations are particularly problematic in experimental settings, where chemists favor incremental, synthetically tractable changes to known compounds. Moreover, while data-driven molecular generators such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) [4, 5, 6] can provide a workaround by learning continuous latent spaces, they require large training datasets and can produce invalid or unrealistic molecules, limiting their utility in early-stage discovery or low-data regimes. To address these limitations, we introduce TuRBO-Mol, a novel trust-region Bayesian optimization algorithm tailored for practical, progressive molecular design. TuRBO-Mol extends the original TuRBO algorithm [7] (originally developed for high-dimensional continuous spaces) to discrete molecular spaces by constructing dynamic trust regions based on Tanimoto similarity between molecular fingerprints. These trust regions adaptively expand when the model discovers better-performing molecules and contract otherwise, enabling localized, sample-efficient exploration that reflects synthetic accessibility. Rather than relying on pre-defined libraries or latent space models, TuRBO-Mol generates candidate molecules on-the-fly via realistic structural perturbations such as atom or functional group substitutions. This search strategy mirrors how chemists reason about chemical modifications, ensuring that candidates remain both valid and synthetically relevant throughout the optimization process. We evaluate TuRBO-Mol on multiple benchmark MPO tasks, demonstrating that it achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer evaluations. Notably, we present what we believe is the first application of trust-region BO to the computational discovery of non-precious metal catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction using density functional theory simulations. Across tasks, TuRBO-Mol consistently produces diverse, high-quality molecules and scales effectively to large, unstructured chemical spaces. These results position TuRBO-Mol as a practical and interpretable approach for molecular design, bridging the gap between theoretical BO and the constraints of real-world chemistry workflows. topic: Feeding Frenzy: A Model-Based Approach to Adaptive Feed Scheduling in Bioprocessing
title: Feeding Frenzy: A Model-Based Approach to Adaptive Feed Scheduling in Bioprocessing
abstract: In traditional fed-batch cell culture processes, feed media is often added as a fixed percentage of the initial post-inoculation volume, regardless of growth performance. This feeding strategy can result in suboptimal feeding, either underfeeding high-performing cell lines or overfeeding low-performing ones. As a result, increased osmolality, nutrient depletion or accumulation of by-products can adversely affect cellular growth and process performance. Instead, adjusting feed rates according to monitored cell densities, ensures a more consistent and controlled bioprocessing environment, ultimately leading to more reliable and reproducible results. In this contribution, we present a dynamic feeding strategy for bioprocess development, which improves upon conventional fixed-percentage feed schedules. By leveraging a mechanistic cell culture model that determines feed additions based on cell densities, we optimized the feeding strategy. The model included a representation of the cell metabolism in CHO cells and the dynamic behavior of cell culture processes inside bioreactors. It is especially enabling the simulation of complex feeding strategies. Based on the process performance of an exemplary model molecule we optimized and studied the impact of various feeding patterns, from constant to variable feed/cell mass ratios. Using this model, promising feeding schedule patterns were identified. In summary, a model-based approach was guiding our feed schedule optimization, and we proceeded to implement these strategies experimentally in small-scale processes. This approach not only provides a more efficient and effective way to manage nutrient supply during cell culture processes but also opens new possibilities for scaling up these optimized feeding schedules to larger bioprocesses and ensures increased reproducibility across scales.

topic: Improved Models for Microwave-Assisted Lyophilization in a Vial
title: Improved Models for Microwave-Assisted Lyophilization in a Vial
abstract: Lyophilization, better known as freeze drying, is a key technology for manufacturing shelf-stable pharmaceuticals such as injectable antibiotics, monoclonal antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates and vaccines. The lyophilization process can be divided into three main phases: freezing, primary drying, and secondary drying. Primary drying constitutes the longest stage of the process, taking as long as a week for some products. Accurate models for heat and mass transfer during the primary drying step of lyophilization are crucial for optimizing the lyophilization process, particularly with respect to drying time and product stability. The literature-standard model treats the sublimation front as planar, with vertical pseudo-steady heat and mass transfer. This approach is simple and, with some empirical fit parameters to describe rarefied porous flow, matches experiment as attested in many literature examples. However, a 1D approach is no longer applicable once heating from the vial walls becomes significant. Microwave heating, a promising addition to lyophilization, may heat a glass vial as much as it heats ice. With an axisymmetric level-set-based model (consisting of 4 coupled PDEs), we assess the non-planarity that wall heating induces in the sublimation front. The behavior predicted by this detailed model allows us to suggest improvements to a recently-published lumped-capacitance model [1], (consisting of 3 ODEs), where we are able to drop an empirical fit parameter. We compare the 2D and lumped capacitance simulations to experimental temperature measurements, validating their utility in further development of microwave-assisted lyophilization technology. topic: Assessing Shortcut Behavior in Tulip Vessels with Lattice Boltzmann Method and Reduced Order Models
title: Assessing Shortcut Behavior in Tulip Vessels with Lattice Boltzmann Method and Reduced Order Models
abstract: Diafiltration and ultrafiltration (UF/DF) are critical processing steps for the production of biomolecules such as proteins. They are often used in tandem: while ultrafiltration increases the concentration of the target product in the solution, diafiltration exchanges the buffer to remove solvents and salts from the solution. Tulip vessels are a popular choice for UF/DF processes because they allow low minimal working volumes for high product concentrations. However, the tulip design has the potential of short-circuiting. Due to this shortcut, a part of the higher product concentration from the retentate flow reaches the feed flow before it is completely mixed in the vessel. The results are unexpectedly high product concentrations, higher viscosity of the solution, poor filter performance and in extreme cases, filter clogging. The shortcut rate depends on operating conditions, such as mixing speed and recirculation flow rate, and material properties. Thus, each process and operating conditions have a characteristic shortcut rate. In this work, we focus on the diafiltration step. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has become the tool of choice for the numerical study of mixing processes inside stirred tanks [1]. In the presented work, we have used an in-house CFD code based on Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM). Beside the fluid flow calculation, a passive scalar equation has been implemented to track the protein concentrations. In the presented work, we have defined the shortcut rate as a difference between the concentration at tank outlet surface and volume averaged concentration inside the tank. Larger concentration at outlet surface as inside the tank, identified the shortcut. In the simulation, the shortcut is calculated using a tracer and passive scalar respectively. At the beginning, the tracer concentration in the tank volume is set to zero and at the outlet equal to one. The difference between these two concentrations is monitored. This difference peaks at the start of the process and reduces over time to zero when perfect mixing is achieved. The diafiltration process itself requires long process times in the order of hours. Thus, the results of the LBM simulations are used to parametrize a reduced order model. The reduced order model is a reactor network model with a feedback loop: The concentration at the vessel inlet (filter retentate flow) depends on the concentration at the vessel outlet (filter feed flow). The reduced order model predicts the time to exchange the buffer, and the expected increase in product concentration at the outlet surface during diafiltration. The LBM simulations yielded shortcut rates in the range of 10%-30% for a given set of operating conditions. Choosing process conditions with a higher throughput at the cost of increased shortcut behavior can be a valid process design decision to reduce the process time. The reduced order model quantifies the increase in product concentration and the relative increase in process time due to the shortcut, allowing for better process design decisions. topic: Modeling Oxidation of Copper Needles As an Animal Health Supplement: Mixing and Optimization of a Rotating Drum Reactor
title: Modeling Oxidation of Copper Needles As an Animal Health Supplement: Mixing and Optimization of a Rotating Drum Reactor
abstract: Copper is an essential trace mineral required for various physiological functions in animals, including enzyme activity, immune response, and red blood cell formation. Copper oxide needles have been developed as an effective and targeted supplement, which provides a slow-release source of copper, reducing their risk of toxicity while ensuring prolonged availability of the mineral. Their use is particularly beneficial in ruminants such as cattle, sheep, and goats, helping to improve growth rates, fertility, and overall health [1]. The production of copper oxide needles is typically carried out in rotating drums involving a controlled thermal oxidation process of copper containing materials. The prepared high-purity copper material is placed into rotating drums, where it undergoes controlled heating in an oxygen-rich environment. The drum’s rotation is to achieve uniform exposure of the material to heat and oxygen, leading to the gradual formation of copper oxides (Cu₂O and CuO). The rotation of the drum helps to prevent agglomeration under high temperatures, ensuring that the needles remain well-separated and uniformly sized. Process parameters such as temperature, rotation speed, and oxygen flow need to be carefully monitored to optimize the process, with an eye towards reducing manufacturing costs of this animal supplement. A Discrete Element Method (DEM) model has been used to simulated needle mixing behavior inside a rotating drum and virtually experiment different reactor designs. Initial reactor design has been studied to predict long-term processing times using a Reduced Order Model (based on a Markov chain approach [2]) and considering three compartments, surface, free-falling zones and the bed. Statistics on particle trajectories computed from DEM simulations are used as model input: the DEM model estimates the duration that needles will spend in the oxidation zones during processing under different configurations. Experimental data for the smallest batch size (40 kg) serves as a reference for the processing time required to reach the desired levels of oxidation of the copper needles, and the process end-time for larger batches is then predicted using the compartment model. The study identified key differences in mixing behavior across various batch sizes for the existing equipment and newly proposed designs that aimed to ensure needles remain well-separated and uniformly distributed. A five-fold reduction in processing time, with a consequential decrease in the production costs, was achieved by implementing specific baffles design. Finally, the study concludes with a summary of key project outcomes and recommendations for successful process optimization and increased production capacity. References [1] Suttle NF, 1981. topic: De Novo Design of Copolymers with Desired Properties Using Large Language Models
title: De Novo Design of Copolymers with Desired Properties Using Large Language Models
abstract: Copolymers, composed of two or more monomer units, enable tunable material properties essential for applications in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and electronics, where high glass transition temperature (T g ) is critical for stability and performance. Traditional copolymer design relies on decades of trial-and-error experiments, but the vast chemical space and structural complexity of copolymers make such approaches inefficient. While recent advancements in computational methods have emerged as promising tools for copolymer design, they primarily focus on copolymers' property prediction and are constrained by the lack of public copolymer databases, limiting their ability to support inverse design for property-targeted copolymers. Here, we presented an automated large language model (LLM)-based framework for the de novo design of copolymers with desired thermal properties. We first applied LLMs to extract compositional and thermal information from 393 copolymer articles automatically, creating a public dataset of 1195 entries with a high extracted accuracy (F1 score=0.8043) 1 . Using this dataset, we trained machine learning models to predict T g , achieving high accuracy (the R 2 reached 0.83 on the additional test dataset). We then developed a conditional generative model based on the minGPT architecture to design copolymers with high T g values 2 . Totally, we generated 2928 valid copolymer candidates, with a significant 192.9% improvement in average T g . Finally, molecular dynamics simulations were performed to validate the T g values of four newly generated copolymers, which showed an average related error of 10.07% between the predicted and MD-validated values. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the potential of LLM-driven approaches to accelerate the inverse design of functional copolymers. References: 1. Khalighinejad G, Circi D, Brinson LC, Dhingra B. topic: Polymer-Grafted Nanoparticles for Ceramics: Thermal Treatment Effects on Dynamics, Rheology, and Char Yield
title: Polymer-Grafted Nanoparticles for Ceramics: Thermal Treatment Effects on Dynamics, Rheology, and Char Yield
abstract: Preceramic polymer grafted nanoparticles (PCPGNPs) offer unique advantages over other preceramic materials, including increased ceramic yield, controlled particle arrangement, and reduced volume shrinkage and mass loss. This study investigates the effects of low-temperature thermal treatments on the material transformations of PCPGNPs with a silica nanoparticle core and poly(1,1-dimethylpropylsilnae) corona suspended in SMP-877. The addition of PCPGNPs to SMP-877 increased the elastic modulus and viscosity, with percolation occurring between 50-60 wt% PCPGNP. Above this concentration, the particles formed a space-spanning network. Rheological and X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) measurements during thermal treatments demonstrated the effect of crosslinking on the resulting moduli and dynamics. When the neat PCPGNP grafts overlapped, the moduli increased, and a jammed state persisted even when cooled to room temperature, likely contributing to increased char yield. Understanding the thermal treatment of these hybrid materials is crucial for advancing their applications in turbine engines, advanced friction, and heat-shielding components.

topic: Polarized Soft X-Ray Scattering (PRSoXS) Measures Tunable Interfacial Molecular Orientation in Phase-Separated Organic Thin Films
title: Polarized Soft X-Ray Scattering (PRSoXS) Measures Tunable Interfacial Molecular Orientation in Phase-Separated Organic Thin Films
abstract: Control over phase separation and molecular orientation in organic thin films is critical to design effective and stable organic electronic materials. Different preferred structures and mobilities at the free and buried interfaces impact both the molecular organization during the non-equilibrium deposition process and the ultimate function and stability over the lifetime of a device. It can be difficult to simultaneously engineer both the compositional phase separation and the molecular orientation; moreover, it can be difficult to measure the two structural parameters in all-organic blends. Here, we use physical vapor deposition (PVD) to co-deposit blends of organic semiconductors into films with thicknesses ranging from 20 to 300 nanometers. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is used to quantify phase separation and height fluctuations at the free surface. Transmission Polarized Resonant Soft X-ray Scattering (PRSoXS) measures hierarchical phase-separated structure through the bulk of the thin films and reveals a surprisingly high degree of in-plane molecular orientation at the interface between components. The in-plane interfacial orientation depends strongly on the film thickness, deposition temperature, and deposition rate. The PRSoXS is interpreted using a computational scattering simulation framework which quantifies the magnitude and length of the molecular orientation and the purity of domains. The two techniques show increasing length scales of phase separation with decreasing film thickness at both the free surface and through the bulk, suggesting that the films are uniformly phase-separated throughout their thickness. The thin films show enhanced kinetic and thermal stability similar to that of homogeneous single- and multi-component vapor-deposited glasses [1]. Our results suggest that cooperative molecular orientation and phase separation are highly correlated, and that strong ordering can be induced over long length scales by physical vapor deposition. We show that vapor depositing into highly confined films can prepare new morphologies that are inaccessible when depositing thicker films, as has been recently shown for single-component vapor-deposited glasses [2] and is shown for the first time here for multiple components. Our work may enable design rules to make thin organic films with finely controlled phase separation and molecular orientation, which can be used to optimize properties for organic electronic applications. Furthermore, the measurement and analysis framework used throughout this work strengthens the information available from the PRSoXS technique, which can be used and expanded to measure nm-scale interfacial features in a wide range of soft matter systems. topic: ProcedureT5: Enhanced Experimental Procedure Prediction with Pre-Training and Data Augmentation
title: ProcedureT5: Enhanced Experimental Procedure Prediction with Pre-Training and Data Augmentation
abstract: Computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) has demonstrated its potential to assist the synthesis of target molecules by proposing synthetic pathways 1 , recommending reaction conditions 2 , and assessing the likelihood of success for the proposed reactions 3 . However, translating computer-generated synthesis routes into executable experimental procedures remains a challenge due to the lack of robust automated methods. To meet the demand for automated experimental procedure prediction, AI-driven data extraction has been used to mitigate the limited availability of annotated experimental procedure data, enabling the curation of datasets for developing experimental procedure prediction models 4–6 . Despite the efficiency of AI-driven data extraction, model performance in this domain demands further improvement and rigorous evaluation beyond AI-curated test sets, necessitating advanced training frameworks and high-quality benchmarks. In this work, we introduce ProcedureT5, an approach that integrates chemistry-oriented pre-trained models with augmented multi-source datasets to enhance the prediction of experimental procedures across broader scenarios. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Pistachio dataset - a collection of reaction procedures derived from US patent literature, showing a 4-point increase in BLEU score and a 34% improvement in exact-match accuracy compared to existing methods. Additionally, we curate a small expert-annotated dataset, Orgsyn, consisting of verified organic synthesis procedures, to assess the model’s performance in more diverse applications. Fine-tuning ProcedureT5 on the Orgsyn dataset demonstrates its adaptability, yielding a BLEU score of 41.19 and an average similarity of 50.58%. This work underscores the crucial role of ProcedureT5 in bridging the gap between computational synthesis planning and practical laboratory implementation. topic: Application of Hybrid Dynamic Modelling for Fed-Batch Cell Culture Processes Using Gaussian Process Regression
title: Application of Hybrid Dynamic Modelling for Fed-Batch Cell Culture Processes Using Gaussian Process Regression
abstract: The development of dynamic process models provides an indispensable approach for capturing the intricate, time-dependent behaviour of biological processes, particularly in dynamic systems such as fed-batch Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell cultures [1-4]. Dynamic models help bridge the gap between experimental observations and process understanding, allowing for improved design and performance predictions during process development. However, accurately modelling the complexities of cellular processes, including cell growth, death, and metabolism, remains a significant challenge due to the non-linear nature of these systems and the inherent variability in bioprocess experimental data [5]. This study presents a hybrid dynamic process model that integrates Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) for estimating cell-specific rates, coupled with material balance equations to capture the underlying dynamics of CHO fed-batch cell culture processes. The principal aim of this research is to investigate how specific properties of the GPR model, such as data smoothing, kernel function selection, and input feature selection, affect GPR performance, and how these properties influence the predictive capability when integrated into a larger dynamic process model. By focusing on these GPR-specific attributes, this work aims to advance current understanding of how model development choices impact the overall performance of hybrid dynamic models within bioprocessing applications. The exploration of key GPR model properties in this study is driven by the need to maximise the predictive capacity of dynamic models while accounting for the complexity and variability of biological data. Firstly, the role of data smoothing techniques prior to rate estimation is investigated, to assess potential impact on model accuracy. Secondly, the study explores the relevance of kernel selection, through comprehensive comparison of Squared Exponential (SE), Matern, and Rational Quadratic (RQ) kernel options, to understand the influence on model performance and generalisability. Finally, the study evaluates the impact of input feature selection, particularly the importance of leveraging domain-specific knowledge to identify critical model features that contribute towards improved prediction. To complement primary investigations, the study employs global sensitivity analysis (GSA) to provide an understanding on how different input features contribute to model variance, thus providing deeper insight into the most influential factors on cell-specific rate estimates. While a strategy for applying GSA to advanced regression models, such as GPR, has not been published to date, the results indicate that variance-based approaches can lead to enhanced process insight through characterising the distribution of variance in model predictions across input features. Ultimately, the work presented aims to offer valuable insight into the development of accurate and efficient hybrid dynamic models for bioprocess applications. By carefully examining the impact of GPR model properties on predictive performance, this work highlights the importance of balancing model complexity and predictive accuracy. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge in dynamic bioprocess modelling, particularly in the context of fed-batch cell culture processes, while providing a strong foundation for future research in dynamic cell culture modelling and the deployment of bioprocess digital twins. topic: Multi-Constrained Molecular Optimization in Transformer-Derived Latent Spaces
title: Multi-Constrained Molecular Optimization in Transformer-Derived Latent Spaces
abstract: Designing molecules that satisfy multiple simultaneous constraints—such as efficacy, solubility, permeability, metabolic stability, and safety—is a fundamental challenge in early-stage drug and material discovery. While generative models like GANs, VAEs, and reinforcement learning-based frameworks have made strides in exploring chemical space, they typically operate by sampling from a learned distribution. As a result, they struggle to solve true multi-objective optimization problems. These models are not inherently designed to enforce multiple property constraints explicitly, often requiring complex and unstable loss formulations or multi-step post-processing. This leads to issues such as poor control over generated properties, limited generalizability to new constraints, and a high risk of generating impractical molecules [1]. To address the limitations of sampling-based generative models, we present a new framework that approaches molecular design as a direct optimization task in the latent space of a transformer-based chemical language model. Rather than generating molecules and filtering them post hoc, our method searches over a continuous, chemically meaningful embedding space where multiple property constraints can be enforced simultaneously and explicitly. This latent space is defined by a transformer encoder pre-trained on large-scale SMILES datasets using masked language modeling [2,3], which produces rich molecular representations that capture both local structural features and broader functional context—without relying on handcrafted descriptors. Optimization is carried out in this latent space using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a metaheuristic algorithm well-suited for navigating high-dimensional, non-convex search spaces [4]. In this setting, each particle represents a candidate molecule in latent space, and its quality is assessed through a suite of neural network-based property predictors. These predictors are trained to estimate key attributes such as lipophilicity, solubility, permeability, metabolic clearance, and toxicity, directly from the latent embeddings. By combining all property requirements into a single composite objective function, the framework guides the search toward embeddings that correspond to chemically valid molecules satisfying multiple target criteria. This structured and constraint-aware optimization process enables more reliable and targeted molecular discovery compared to conventional generative approaches. Once optimal latent vectors are identified, we use a greedy decoding mechanism to reconstruct molecular SMILES from the embeddings, ensuring that generated structures are syntactically valid and chemically meaningful. Unlike traditional generative models, which often require iterative tuning or fine-tuning to meet multiple objectives, our approach enables direct and interpretable optimization in latent space, improving efficiency, scalability, and constraint adherence. A key forward-looking aspect of our work is its integration potential with process modeling. While current efforts focus on optimizing molecular-level properties, many real-world applications demand alignment with process-level metrics—such as ease of formulation, solvent recovery, or separation efficiency. Our framework is designed to interface with simulation tools that model such downstream behavior. By passing predicted molecular properties into process models, we enable system-level evaluation and selection of generated molecules based not only on intrinsic merit but also on real-world functional compatibility. In summary, we introduce a scalable and modular methodology for multi-constrained molecular optimization that overcomes key limitations of existing generative approaches. By combining transformer-based molecular embeddings, metaheuristic optimization, and property-aware decoding—with extensibility toward process modeling—this framework lays the groundwork for more informed, controlled, and application-ready molecular design. title: ML Prediction of High-Affinity Aptamers for Novel Biological Vectors for Biosensor Applications
abstract: Rapid detection and identification of biological pathogens are crucial for fighting contagious pathogens and deterring biological threats. Probes that have both high affinity and specificity to a pathogen are critical for developing and employing biosensors. Single-stranded oligonucleotides have been shown to demonstrate both high affinity and specificity in specific cases. 1,2 The chemical synthesis process for oligonucleotides also alleviates the batch issues associated with peptide and antibody production. 3 While high affinity and specific aptamers can be identified through the process known as Systematic Evolution of Ligands by EXponential (SELEX) enrichment, SELEX and its modified versions are time-consuming, costly, and have a low success rate. 4 To consistently and rapidly identify high affinity and specific aptamers, we proposed a machine learning method to design sequences for specific pathogenic targets. We demonstrate that classical machine learning methods can predict oligonucleotide sequences binding to target proteins. Currently, our focus is on generating a more robust dataset of high affinity oligonucleotides and testing their specificity; the expanded dataset will facilitate development of higher performing machine learning models, such as a graphical neural network. The results of this study will enable rapid design of high affinity oligonucleotides solely based on the target’s amino acid sequence. Corresponding Author: LTC Stephen G. topic: Simulation-Guided Design of a Pharmaceutical Batch Powder Blending Process
title: Simulation-Guided Design of a Pharmaceutical Batch Powder Blending Process
abstract: Achieving homogeneous blends of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and excipients is critical in pharmaceutical tablet manufacturing to ensure consistent dosage and optimal powder processability. Traditionally, developing and scaling up powder blending operations relies on expensive, labor-intensive experimental trials that provide very limited insight into blending dynamics. Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations offer deeper process insights and can significantly reduce experimental costs. In this study, DEM simulations were applied to investigate the blending dynamics of two APIs and various excipients in an industrial-scale pharmaceutical bin blender. Powder components were experimentally characterized using dynamic angle of repose tests. The results were then used to calibrate DEM parameters of three modeled powder components. Simulations of a 25-minute blending operation, including a 20-minute pre-blending stage and a 5-minute final blending step, indicated axial concentration gradients of the APIs. Experimental validation through targeted sampling and HPLC analyses confirmed these simulation predictions. Various strategies to mitigate these API gradients were evaluated using the DEM model. Results indicated that a 90° reorientation of the blending container around the vertical axis prior to the final blending step notably improved axial homogeneity. This approach effectively minimized inhomogeneity with minimal engineering adjustments and could be further modified to drastically reduce the blending time. The findings underscore the effectiveness of calibrated DEM simulations as tools for designing and optimizing pharmaceutical blending processes. This simulation-based methodology provides a robust framework for identifying process risks and testing mitigation strategies, enabling faster, more efficient process development while minimizing costly experimental work.

topic: Stability of a Rigid Particle in Sticky Suspensions Undergoing Shear Flow
title: Stability of a Rigid Particle in Sticky Suspensions Undergoing Shear Flow
abstract: Suspensions of soft particles with short-range attractive interactions are found in many industrial formulations, ranging from food and pharmaceuticals to cosmetics and advanced materials, such as toothpaste and mayonnaise. These particles exert short-range attractive interactions by hydrophobic alkyl chain extensions that can form sticky contacts with other hydrophobic alkyl chain due interactions of the extensions with other neighboring particles. These attractions lead to a weak network structure that increases the material’s yield stress and alters its flow behavior. Undergoing shear deformation, these sticky suspensions show flow instabilities such as shear banding. With increased stickiness, a more non-linear velocity profile is observed. Given this flow behavior, several questions arise regarding the ability of these suspensions to suspend a single rigid particle under its weight in shear flow. In this work, we perform particle dynamics simulations to study the sedimentation of a single rigid particle in a sheared suspension of soft, sticky ones. We examine how interparticle attraction affects the critical applied force required to initiate sedimentation and how this threshold varies with shear rate. Our results show that stickiness not only increases the resistance to sedimentation but also modifies the local flow field near the rigid particle compared to the non-attractive case and the contacts are more uniformly distributed due to the sticky nature. Finally, a stability diagram is constructed to map the transition between stable and sedimenting states as a function of shear rate and applied force at varying degrees of stickiness.
